## I.4 Choosing wisely / Things to avoid
* Pilocarpine may worsen angle closure due to lenticular and retro-lenticular mechanisms.
11) **Do not presume that acute angle closure is always due to pupil block.**
* Shorter eyes are at particular risk of surgical complications and should be planned accordingly.
12) **Do not dismiss axial length measurements in patients with angle closure.**

...

## I.7 Landmark randomised controlled trials for glaucoma
### I.7.2 Treatment vs no treatment trials on angle closure
#### I.7.2.1 Zhongshan Angle Closure Prevention study (ZAP)
* – At 14-years extended follow up, a primary endpoint occurred in 33 LPI-treated eyes (4.27 per 1000 eye-years) and 105 control eyes (13.59 per 1000 eye-years) (p<0.001).
* – LPI was associated with 47% and 69% reduction of relative risk of PAC or AAC after 6 years (HR 0.53) and 14 years (HR 0.31), respectively.
* – One of the LPI-treated eyes developed an acute attack of angle closure whereas 5 did so in control eyes.

...

#### I.7.2.2 The Singapore asymptomatic narrow angles laser iridotomy study (ANA-LIS)
The ANA-LIS Study was an open-label, paired-eye, randomised controlled trial investigating prophylactic LPI versus no treatment in PACS. 480 participants (mostly women and Chinese) with bilateral PACS, defined as irido-trabecular contact of at least 180 degrees without PAS or raised IOP, were randomised to receive LPI in one eye and no treatment in the fellow eye.
The primary outcome was the development of PAC or PACG. The follow up was 5 years.

...

# Part II • **Chapter 1**
## II.1 Patient Examination
### II.1.2 Gonioscopy
The purpose of gonioscopy is to inspect the anterior chamber angle. It is based on the recognition of angle landmarks and must always include an assessment of the following:
* Level of iris insertion, both apparent insertion without indentation and true insertion during indentation
* The shape of the peripheral iris profile, either flat, convex or concave
* Width of the iridocorneal angle between peripheral iris and cornea
* Degree, type and distribution of pigmentation in the trabecular meshwork
* Areas of iridotrabecular apposition or synechia
* Any abnormal or postoperative findings

...

#### II.1.2.1 Anatomy
##### II.1.2.1.1 Reference Landmarks
Indentation (‘dynamic’) gonioscopy helps to visualise TM in angle closure (See Fig II.1.6 ).

...

#### II.1.2.2 Techniques
##### II.1.2.2.2 Dynamic gonioscopy by indentation or compression
[Dynamic indentation gonioscopy. When no angle structure is directly visible before indentation, angle closure may be present, and it can be synechial or appositional (1). If during indentation the iris moves peripherally backwards and the angle recess widens (2), the picture in (1) is to be interpreted as appositional closure and a suspicion of relative pupillary block is raised (2).
When during indentation the angle widens but iris strands remain attached to the angle outer wall (3), the picture in (1) is to be interpreted as synechial closure.

If during indentation the iris moves peripherally backwards and the angle recess widens (2), the picture in (1) is to be interpreted as appositional closure and a suspicion of relative pupillary block is raised (2).
When during indentation the angle widens but iris strands remain attached to the angle outer wall (3), the picture in (1) is to be interpreted as synechial closure. A large and/or anteriorly displaced lens causes the iris to move only slightly and evenly backwards during indentation (4) making the lens a likely component of angle closure.")

...

Dynamic indentation gonioscopy. When no angle structure is directly visible before indentation, angle closure may be present, and it can be synechial or appositional (1). If during indentation the iris moves peripherally backwards and the angle recess widens (2), the picture in (1) is to be interpreted as appositional closure and a suspicion of relative pupillary block is raised (2).

...

#### II.1.2.3 Grading of the anterior chamber angle
##### II.1.2.3.1 Slit lamp-grading of peripheral AC depth- The Van Herick method
This technique is based on the use of corneal thickness as a unit measure of the depth of the anterior chamber at the furthest periphery, preferably on the temporal side. The slit lamp light beam should be at 60 degrees. Grade 0 represents iridocorneal contact, i.e., angle closure.
A space between iris and corneal endothelium of less than 1/4 corneal thickness is interpreted as a high risk of anatomical angle closure. When the space is between 1/4 and 1/2 corneal thickness the grade is 2, with a very low risk of angle closure. A grade 3 is not occludable, with an irido/endothelial distance more than 1/2 corneal thickness.

...

#### II.1.2.4 Anterior segment imaging techniques
Anterior segment imaging such as ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM), anterior segment OCTs (AS-OCT) and Scheimpflug cameras can be useful in some circumstances but cannot replace gonioscopy. Added to gonioscopy, imaging techniques may help elucidate the mechanism of angle closure. UBM can be particularly helpful as – in contrast to AS-OCT – it can image tissues behind the iris (anteriorly placed iris processes in plateau iris, tumours, cysts).
Anterior segment imaging provides quantitative angle measurements and helps document the chamber angle dynamics with different light conditions. Anterior segment imaging may classify more eyes as having angle closure than gonioscopy, thus leading to overdiagnosis. Automated 360° goniophotography is also available.
A recent meta-analysis indicated that AS-OCT was not superior to the Van Herick test in detecting angle closure, OCT for angle evaluation has proven to be useful in virtual clinic settings as it allows for asynchronous evaluation of the angle.

...

# Part II • **Chpater 2**
## II.2 Classification and terminology
### II.2.4 Angle closure
Angle closure can be classified by the mechanism leading to iridotrabecular contact into 4 categories listed from anterior to posterior: 1) at the level of the pupil, 2) at the level of the ciliary body, 3) at the level of lens, and 4) factors behind the lens. Anterior mechanisms (1 and 2) and posterior mechanisms (3 and 4) should be differentiated due to key differences in management.

...

When some resistance to such flow arises, usually at the pupil causing pressure to be higher in the posterior chamber compared to anterior chamber, the iris bows forward and the peripheral iris may touch the trabecular meshwork (TM) causing irido-trabecular contact (ITC). The peripheral and mid-peripheral anterior chamber is typically shallow with the central anterior chamber relatively deep. Pupillary block may also contribute to secondary angle closure, e.g.

...

Aqueous misdirection, also called malignant glaucoma, is an uncommon form of angle closure. The mechanism is uncertain but likely involves increased choroidal volume and impaired fluid movement from posterior to anterior segments with posterior misdirection of aqueous possibly accumulating in the vitreous. The lens/ iris diaphragm is pushed forward and occludes the anterior chamber angle. The anterior chamber is uniformly very shallow.
Aqueous misdirection usually occurs after surgery in eyes with short axial length. IOP may be normal at early stages.
* – Other posterior pushing mechanism, e.g. tumour, retinal gas or oil tamponade, uveal effusion (e.g. spontaneous, drug-induced) may cause angle closure by forward movement of the lens-iris diaphragm which may be variably combined with pupillary block.

...

#### II.2.4.1 Primary angle closure glaucoma
Using AS-OCT, identification of the key landmark of the scleral spur may be difficult in some eyes, as may detection of ciliary processes or PAS. AS-OCT tends to identify more ITC than gonioscopy resulting in false positives. AS-OCT may be useful for demonstrating to patients the mechanism of their problem and for documenting changes in angle width after iridotomy.

...

Provocative tests for angle closure are not recommended. Provocation with pharmacological dilation of the pupil does not mimic physiological conditions and there is no good quality evidence that pharmacological or dark prone provocation tests are useful for identifying high risk individuals. See Fc X and XI.

...

##### II.2.4.1.1 Primary angle closure suspect (PACS)
Treatment options for PACS include observation or LPI. In the ZAP study, LPI halved the risk of new angle closure disease (defined as raised IOP and/or new PAS) at 6 years but the rate was low, even in untreated eyes, and there were no cases of glaucoma. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of raised IOP and/or new PAS was 44 over 6 years.
Similarly, in the ANA-LIS trial, the overall progression rate to PAC or PACG was very low and untreated PACS eyes had twice the risk of developing endpoints, mostly PAS, over 5 years. The NNT benefit of prophylactic LPI for PAC and/ or PACG in the ANA-LIS study was 22 patients to prevent a single endpoint in 1 patient over 5 years.

...

urgent eye care. Patients with untreated PACS should be advised to have regular eye examinations and avoid pharmacologic pupil dilatation. Information should be provided about symptoms of acute angle closure with advice given to seek prompt attention should they occur. Following LPI, it is important to repeat gonioscopy and reevaluate the angle. Persistence of ITC after LPI may be useful to risk stratify patients.
Gonioscopy should be repeated in phakic patients even after LPI since the angle will progressively narrow with age-related enlargement of the lens.

...

##### II.2.4.1.4 Acute angle closure (AAC)
Pupillary block is the most common mechanism, but it is crucial to exclude secondary causes of angle closure (e.g., plateau iris, aqueous misdirection). Whilst pupil-block is treated with pilocarpine, lens-induced and retro-lenticular causes of acute angle closure should be treated with cycloplegia (e.g. atropine, tropicamide or cyclopentolate) and may be worsened by pilocarpine. Typically AAC will not resolve spontaneously.

...

Examine the patient and take a focused history to exclude secondary, lens-induced or retro-lenticular causes. As a high proportion of acute angle closure episodes are precipitated by either topical or systemic medications, it is essential to take a thorough history of prescription and non-prescription medications and determine any medication allergies. Topical and systemic medication should be given to lower IOP and help clear the cornea.

...

Immediate treatment of AAC should include topical IOP lowering medications with aqueous suppressants preferrable. Prostaglandin analogues have a slower onset of action and are less useful in the acute setting. If pupil block is suspected topical pilocarpine 2% should be given. Pilocarpine may be ineffective if IOP is markedly raised, or the iris is ischaemic so should be deferred until IOP is reduced if presenting IOP is ≥40 mmHg.
Pupil constriction tends to occur only when IOP has been lowered. Miotics in large doses can cause systemic side effects including abdominal spasms and sweating; therefore intensive use of pilocarpine should be avoided. Pilocarpine can also cause forward movement of the iris-lens diaphragm, further shallowing the anterior chamber and is contraindicated in lens- induced and retro-lenticular mechanisms of angle closure.

...

Phacoemulsification following acute angle closure is generally challenging due to the shallow AC, large lens, corneal oedema, poorly dilated pupil, frequent posterior synechiae, lower corneal endothelial cell counts and weaker zonules. It is useful to perform biometry (e.g. axial length, AC depth) following acute angle closure to better understand the anatomical predisposition contributing to the acute attack and gauge the risk of surgery.

...

##### II.2.4.1.5 Status post-acute angle closure
Acute angle closure may occur secondary to pharmacological pupil dilation, however, in the overall population it is generally safe. The risk of missing sight- threatening retinal conditions because of inadequate fundal examination through undilated pupils far outweighs the risk of precipitating angle closure induced by diagnostic mydriasis.

...

Pilocarpine should not be used to preventively re-constrict the pupil after dilation as it may immobilize the pupil in a mid-dilated position, increasing the risk of angle closure.

...

### II.2.5 Secondary angle closure
#### II.2.5.2 Secondary angle closure with anterior “pulling” mechanism synechial closure without pupillary block
Aetiology/mechanism :
The TM is obstructed by iris tissue or a membrane. The iris and/or a membrane are progressively pulled forward to occlude the angle.

...

##### II.2.5.2.4 Aqueous misdirection or malignant glaucoma
Treatment :
Medical treatment
* – Parasympatholytics (atropine or cyclopentolate)
* – Aqueous production suppressants given orally and/or topically
* – Hyperosmotics
* – Miotics are contraindicated
Surgical treatment

...

##### II.2.5.2.9 Congenital anomalies associated with secondary angle closure glaucoma
Gonioscopy should be repeated, and the angle reassessed periodically during follow-up in all phakic patients.

...

# Part II • **Chpater 3**
## II.3 Treatment
### II.3.8 Glaucoma management during pregnancy or breast- feeding
Although results from animal studies of IOP-lowering medications have reported adverse effects, the overall level of evidence for the risk to pregnant women and fetus/infants is low. For beta-blockers and pilocarpine there is considerable experience and they are generally considered safe.

...

### II.3.12 Laser surgery
#### II.3.12.1 Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI)
Instil topical pilocarpine. If the cornea is oedematous, use topical glycerin 10% if available. Systemic acetazolamide, IV mannitol or oral hyperosmotic agents may be needed to clear the cornea in cases of AAC. For prevention of IOP spikes use a topical alpha-2 agonist 1 hour prior to the procedure and immediately afterwards.

...

#### II.3.12.2 Laser trabeculoplasty
Abundant instillation of topical anesthetic. For prevention of IOP spikes, medications to lower the IOP are recommended. Options include topical alpha-2 agonist (most commonly), pilocarpine or acetazolamide prior to or immediately after the procedure.

...

#### II.3.12.3 Thermal laser peripheral iridoplasty (TLPI)
Instillation of pilocarpine. For prevention of IOP spikes use topical alpha-2 agonist prior to the procedure and immediately afterwards.
Lens:
Contact TLPI lenses.

## Abstract

**Foreword**

We practice medicine in times of exponentially increasing medical knowledge. In 1950, it was estimated that the doubling time was 50 years; by 1980, it was 7 years and by 2010, 3.5 years. In 2020, it was projected to be just 73 days! To continue to practice evidence-based medicine and to provide the best possible care for our patients, clinicians need to adapt their strategies to keep their knowledge up to date. There will always be a role for critical appraisal of individual studies in the field of a clinician’s practice, but with such an increase in the volume of published research, it becomes impossible to appraise all relevant material. For this reason, sources of distilled knowledge, such as the EGS Guidelines, become essential references for best practice medicine.

Rigorous methods for evidence synthesis, such as the systematic reviews overseen by Cochrane, provide a comprehensive summary of the current state of knowledge for important clinical questions. However, for many clinical uncertainties, there is little or no high-quality evidence, let alone an evidence synthesis. Where evidence is lacking, practice guidance needs to be built from expert opinion and consensus, while acknowledging the limitations of such an approach. Expert opinion, derived from sound medical knowledge and years of practice experience, also has an important role in understanding the relevance of lines of evidence and the nuances of implementing them in practice. Thus, the expert commentary around the evidence base given in these Guidelines is essential for proper implementation of published evidence. Importantly, the EGS Guidelines also include ‘Choosing wisely’ elements indicating actions which should be avoided due to insufficient evidence and/or unsubstantiated belief.

Guidelines need regular updating to take account of new knowledge and aspects of clinical care that have not been given sufficient emphasis in the past. This 6th Edition of the EGS Guidelines includes an updated ‘evidence based’ section with new clinical questions and evidence-based answers. The section ‘What matters to patients’ has also been updated, recognising that, because Guidelines are typically written by clinicians for clinicians, there have been gaps in understanding the patient perspective. The updated section now has direct input from the Expert by Experience patient advisors in the EGS Patient Involvement Project and includes eight Tips for Doctors in their communication with patients.

The Guidelines team, led by Drs Pazos, Traverso and Viswanathan, is to be congratulated for the 6th Edition of the Guidelines, updating and enhancing the previous edition, while maintaining the highly success format which gives a framework for glaucoma care, based on evidence synthesis and consensus expert opinion, and presented as a ‘How to’ manual for patient diagnosis and management.

David (Ted) Garway-Heath

Glaucoma UK Professor of Ophthalmology, UCL

Embedded Image

**Introduction**

The European Glaucoma Society Guidelines are at the heart of our educational mission serving not only our members, but all involved in glaucoma care. Previous editions have been among the most widely accessed documents in the field, helping navigate the growing complexity of glaucoma research and clinical practice.

This sixth edition reaffirms our commitment to evidence-based, patient-centred care. It builds on the solid foundations of past editions while embracing key innovations that reflect new scientific insights, emerging technologies, and evolving priorities in glaucoma care.

For the first time, we collaborated closely with patient representatives through the Experts by Experience (EbE) group. Their contributions helped shape clinical questions and emphasized the importance of empathy, communication, and psychological support in managing glaucoma.

The Guidelines maintain a dual purpose: to answer clinically relevant questions through a rigorous evidence-based approach, and to offer comprehensive, practical knowledge for daily use. We have updated existing recommendations and added new topics, including artificial intelligence, cost-effectiveness, adherence strategies, and paediatric glaucoma. A new “Choosing Wisely” section provides clear guidance to avoid low-value interventions. We extend our heartfelt thanks to all contributors and collaborators. This includes the many colleagues who authored and reviewed chapters with great care and expertise, the patient representatives who generously shared their lived experiences, and the team at the University of Genoa, who worked tirelessly to refine content and layout, ensuring clarity and consistency throughout.

A very special word of thanks goes to the Editors Marta Pazos, Carlo Traverso, and Ananth Viswanathan, whose relentless dedication, critical oversight, and countless hours of work were instrumental in shaping the high quality and coherence of this edition. Their leadership and perseverance have been extraordinary. Together, these collective efforts have made this edition a cornerstone of our vision: to foster innovation, strengthen education, enhance communication, and promote best practices in glaucoma care across Europe and beyond.

Ingeborg Stalmans and Luis Abegao Pinto

## Part I

### Background to Guideline Development

### I.1 Background to Guideline Development

These Guidelines aim to support ophthalmologists in managing people with, or at risk of, glaucoma, and to provide useful information to trainees. In the previous 5th edition, we identified and answered 11 clinically relevant questions. To update this section for this 6th edition, we also followed again the grading of recommendations, assessment, development, and evaluations (GRADE) methodology ( [https://gdt.gradepro.org/app/ handbook/handbook.html](https://gdt.gradepro.org/app/handbook/handbook.html) ). We asked the EGS members and the EGS Experts by Experience (EbE-EGS patients’ committee) group to identify key clinical questions on glaucoma care. Specifically we sent an online Survey to all EGS members in September 2024 and to EbE-EGS in October 2024, asking them to confirm if questions from the 5th edition were still important and to provide feedback on the previous questions and also to propose new key question topics, for example, diagnosis, prognosis, and interventions for primary open-angle glaucoma. The Guidelines Task Force subsequently identified the most common topics and prioritised them.

Evidence to inform these Guidelines was gathered in 2024 in collaboration with the USA-Cochrane Eyes and Vision Group by conducting an overview of systematic reviews on glaucoma interventions, prognosis, and diagnosis. Similar to the last edition, a grading system for rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendation, following the grading of recommendations, assessment, development, and evaluations (GRADE), has been used only to answer our final key questions. The remainder of the recommendations and suggestions throughout the text are consensus-based among experts.

As in the previous edition, we provided only references to high-quality systematic reviews, landmark glaucoma trials, and population-based studies with a preference for European-based studies.

Patients’ care and well-being are at the core of our values, and we collaborated side by side with the EGS EbE group to include the patient’s perspective throughout the Guidelines, e.g., identifying key clinical questions, including a do’s and don’ts section for doctors as well as a new chapter about the paediatric glaucoma patients’ most frequent concerns. Material used to develop the Guidelines is available online.

**The European Glaucoma Society (EGS) Guidelines should be considered as guidance rather than strict decision-making protocols.**

Decision-making ultimately should be individualised to the patient’s needs and circumstances, ideally guided by the best available evidence.

The European Glaucoma Society (EGS) and all contributors disclaim responsibility and all liability for any adverse medical or legal effects resulting directly or indirectly from the use of any of the definitions, diagnostic techniques, treatments or protocols described in the Guidelines. The EGS does not endorse any product, procedure, company or organisation.

### I.2 Mission statement

“The goal of care for people with or at risk of glaucoma is to promote their well-being and quality of life (QoL) within a sustainable healthcare system.”

Well-being and QoL are influenced by a person’s visual function, the psychological impact of having a chronic progressive sight-threatening condition and the costs as well as side-effects of treatments. Costs include inconveniences to the individual and their caregivers as well as the financial cost of examinations, diagnostic procedures and therapies, both to the individual and society. The effect of visual function on well-being and QoL is variable; in general, early to moderate glaucoma has only a modest influence, whereas advanced visual function loss in both eyes may considerably reduce QoL.

### I.3 Key questions and evidence-based recommendations

#### I.3.1 New questions for this edition

**Q1. What risk factors should we consider when we assess a person with or at risk of glaucoma?**

Recommendation:

Risk of disease:

Patients with higher IOP (particularly those with pseudoexfoliation), non-white ethnicity (particularly black), older age, family history of glaucoma, myopes are at higher risk for the development of glaucoma. Other risk factors may include: blood pressure dysregulation, cardiovascular disease. In OHT, older age and higher IOP were consistently associated with glaucoma conversion.

Disease progression:

Higher IOP, pseudoexfoliation, older age, presence of disc hemorrhages, and thinner CCT.

Level of evidence : high

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

There is some evidence that some patients over-treated for systemic hypertension may be at increased risk of glaucoma and VF loss. Data from the literature on diabetes, systemic high blood pressure, migraine, Raynaud syndrome, Alzheimer´s disease and H. pylori infections are inconsistent. There is no compelling evidence that diet and lifestyle factors influence glaucoma (see Ch II.3.7 ).

**Q2. What is the recommended first-line treatment for POAG?**

Recommendation :

It is recommended to initiate the treatment for IOP lowering with monotherapy (see Ch II.3.4 , Fc XVII , XVIII and XIX ). Laser trabeculoplasty is also a good option for first-line treatment (see Ch II.3.12.2 ). Patients with high IOPs, e.g., high 20s or above or severe disease may need a more intensive initial treatment e.g. combination of drugs, laser or surgery.

Level of evidence : high

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment

One high quality trial showed that SLT is at least as effective as eye drops. Laser trabeculoplasty should be considered as an option for initial treatment in patients with mild or moderate open angle glaucoma or OHT. There is no evidence regarding effectiveness of trabeculoplasty in patients with severe glaucoma and pigmentary glaucoma (PG). SLT and argon laser trabeculoplasty (ALT) have similar efficacy and are more effective in people with higher IOP.

Factors such as co-morbidities, systemic therapy, adherence, ability to administer drops, patient preference, cost, and availability should be considered.

**Q3. What is the most effective IOP-lowering medication?**

Recommendation: Prostaglandin analogs (PGAs) are the most effective medication, and they are usually recommended as first-choice medical treatment for open-angle glaucoma.

Level of evidence : high

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

There is no difference in IOP lowering between preservative and preservative-free treatments. Preservative-free medications are probably associated with better ocular surface and tolerability, but they are more costly. Further research comparing original and generic PGAs is needed to confirm equivalence.

Factors like possible adverse effects, co-morbidities, systemic therapy, adherence, patient preferences, life expectancy, cost, and availability should be considered in selecting a drug for a given patient. Patients need to be informed about the options that are available and what is best suited for them.

**Q4. How can clinicians help patients adhere to the medical treatment?**

Recommendation :

Simplified regimen, education, effective communication (e.g., asking open questions), alarms/messages.

Level of evidence : very low

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

Tailored care may improve adherence to glaucoma medication. A multidisciplinary approach may yield additional improvements.

**Q5. What is the recommended surgical treatment for non-advanced open- angle glaucoma?**

Recommendation :

Trabeculectomy remains the most effective glaucoma surgery in terms of IOP lowering. Stand-alone MIGS techniques mainly aim to reduce the IOP and/or the medication burden in patients with early to moderate open-angle glaucoma. Bleb- forming techniques have the potential for greater IOP reduction when compared to MIGS.

Level of evidence : High for trabeculectomy; Low for stand-alone MIGS and alternative bleb-forming surgeries.

Strength of recommendation : Strong

Comment :

Glaucoma surgery should be considered whenever medical or laser treatment is unlikely to maintain sight in the glaucomatous eye.

**Q6. What is the recommended surgical treatment for advanced open-angle glaucoma?**

Recommendation :

In advanced open glaucoma, trabeculectomy is the most effective glaucoma surgery to obtain low target IOPs. Trabeculectomy can be offered as a primary intervention.

Level of evidence: high

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

Trabeculectomy has obtained better IOP and VF outcomes when compared to medical therapy. MIGS are not usually indicated for patients with advanced glaucoma. Other bleb-forming surgeries can be used for advanced glaucoma.

**Q7. What is the recommended approach for patients with early or moderate open-angle glaucoma and visually significant cataracts?**

Recommendations :

* – IOP at or near target: Phacoemulsification alone or phacoemulsification with MIGS.
* – IOP significantly above target: Glaucoma intervention should be offered. Bleb-forming surgery with or without phacoemulsification is advisable.

Level of evidence : high

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

Cataract surgery alone is not recommended for controlling glaucoma, although it can modestly but consistently reduce IOP and medications in POAG, with a more pronounced effect in eyes with PXG and higher preoperative IOP values. When making a treatment recommendation, clinicians should consider the benefits of early MIGS surgery in the context of the patient characteristics (medical and non-medical, lifestyle, expectations, etc). Combined procedures using MIGS can moderately lower IOP and reduce medication use. For more severe glaucoma or cases with high preoperative IOP, a bleb-forming surgery such as trabeculectomy is preferred.

Since the success rate for bleb-forming procedures is higher when performed alone than when combined with cataract surgery, performing cataract surgery first is advisable if the clinical condition allows.

**Q8. What is the recommended approach for patients with advanced open-angle glaucoma and visually significant cataracts?**

Recommendations :

* – IOP at target: Phacoemulsification alone is a good option; phacoemulsification may be combined with MIGS as an opportunity to lower IOP more or to reduce drop burden.
* – IOP above target: Glaucoma intervention should be offered. Bleb-forming surgery with or without phacoemulsification is advisable.

Level of evidence : low

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

For more severe glaucoma or cases with high preoperative IOP, a bleb-forming surgery like trabeculectomy is preferred. Since the success rate for bleb-forming procedures is higher when performed alone than when combined with cataract surgery, performing cataract surgery first may be advisable if the clinical condition allows.

**Q9. Are neuroprotective agents or alternative treatments recommended?**

Recommendation :

There is no evidence to support that acupuncture, cannabinoids, or alternative treatments have a role to play in glaucoma management. There is not enough evidence to recommend the use of neuroprotective agents in glaucoma.

Level of evidence : low

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

Oral supplementation of citicoline and nicotinamide are currently being tested in large clinical trials as potential neuroprotective adjuvants for glaucoma management.

**Q10. What is the recommended frequency of testing and monitoring?**

Recommendation :

There is no evidence regarding which combination of tests or testing frequency improves patient outcomes at a sustainable cost. See recommended tests for diagnosis and monitoring in flow chart IX. Follow-up intervals of less than 1 year for ocular hypertension are unlikely to be cost-effective. Increasing the frequency may be needed based on various factors such as glaucoma severity, faster progression rate, non-achievement of target IOP, presence of other high-risk factors, the need for a second test to establish baseline values for future comparisons, or suspicion of artifacts.

Level of evidence : low

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

Most publications and test progression software are based on the assumption that at least five tests i.e. two baseline and three follow-up tests are needed to detect probable progression, and a minimum of two years is necessary to obtain a representative numerical progression rate. Other studies have found that performing two to three tests per year may be sufficient to detect fast-progressors in clinical practice.

**Q11. Is AI recommended for glaucoma management?**

Recommendation :

Although they have promising potential, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of AI algorithms in current clinical practice.

Level of evidence : low

Strength of recommendation : strong

Comment :

Challenges in generalisability, data privacy and ownership, explainability and interpretability must be addressed before widespread clinical adoption. AI has the potential to aid glaucoma diagnosis and detection of progression and may allow screening to be more cost-effective. Additionally, AI tools may be useful for patient risk profiling and predicting future developments. Clinical trials are ongoing to better evaluate its real-world utility and future clinical implementation.

### I.4 Choosing wisely / Things to avoid

Embedded Image

* 1) **Do not use in clinical practice research results derived from samples which do not adequately represent your patient.**
* 2) **Do not perform Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) routinely in otherwise healthy Primary Angle-Closure Suspect (PACS) eyes.**
  
  LPI is advisable only in high-risk PACS eyes (e.g. higher baseline IOP, high hypermetropia, antidepressants or benzodiazepines use, patients that need frequent pupil dilation).
* 3) **Do not perform clear lens extraction in patients below 50 years of age with angle closure at low risk of visual loss.**
  
  Evidence suggests that clear lens extraction is a valid first line intervention for a specific group of PAC patients, e.g. those with high IOP and above 50 years of age.
* 4) **Do not use anterior chamber angle imaging as a replacement for gonioscopy.**
  
  The accuracy of anterior segment imaging in diagnosing angle closure is uncertain. Imaging misses relevant information (e.g. pigmentation) and angle closure features (e.g. peripheral anterior synechia or ciliary processes)
* 5) **Do not correct IOP measurements with CCT-based algorithms.**
  
  They are not validated and should be avoided.
* 6) **Do not focus optic disc assessment on cup/disc ratio.**
  
  Observe the ONH directly with slit lamp or direct ophthalmoscope checking disc appearance, size, shape and the thickness and colour of the rim. A green filter light can help to observe RNFL around the optic disc.
* 7) **Do not diagnose glaucoma based on OCT only.**
  
  OCT on its own does not provide a clinical diagnosis of glaucoma, just a statistical deviation from a reference database.
* 8) **Do not make clinical decisions based on AI only.**
  
  Technologies may support but do not replace clinical judgment.
* 9) **Do not offer genotyping routinely to all POAG patients.**
  
  Individuals from families with multiple members affected with POAG at a relatively young age should be offered the opportunity to undergo genetic testing for MYOC mutations.
* 10) **Do not rely on neuroprotective strategies over IOP-lowering therapies.**
  
  Treatment priority should be reaching the target IOP with established hypotensive therapies.
* 11) **Do not presume that acute angle closure is always due to pupil block.**
  
  Pilocarpine may worsen angle closure due to lenticular and retro-lenticular mechanisms.
* 12) **Do not dismiss axial length measurements in patients with angle closure.**
  
  Shorter eyes are at particular risk of surgical complications and should be planned accordingly.
* 13) **Do not perform further interventions in blind painless eyes with high IOP.**
  
  Once the vision is lost, there is no need to perform further interventions except for painful eyes when pain is due to high IOP.
* 14) **Do not consider MIGS as a procedure without risks or costs.**
* 15) **Do not use MIGS on a rapidly worsening patient**
  
  MIGS are mostly used in to offer the opportunity to mildly lower the IOP and decrease medications in patients with OSD, poor tolerance, or poor compliance.

### I.5 What matters to patients

See Fc I

#### I.5.1 Anxiety associated with glaucoma

The time of first diagnosis - especially when unexpected - is an obvious moment of anxiety for patients, and one which can be mitigated by the provision of support or more information. Empathy with the patient is particularly important when providing a diagnosis; trying to understand what they are thinking and feeling and giving them plenty of opportunity to ask questions and express their fears. The patient may not understand everything at the first consultation, and it may be helpful to repeat information.

Anxiety does not dissipate once the shock of diagnosis has passed: concerns about future deterioration in sight, about ability to hold a driving license, about difficulties with healthcare provision and about age-related difficulty in managing treatment are all common. The perception of disease is likely influenced by family history and how other family members have been affected by glaucoma.

Also, the risk of the patient’s own children inheriting the disease is a concern.

A diagnosis of glaucoma is therefore to be confirmed to the patient when full certainty exists. It is essential to clarify what glaucoma suspect and/or ocular hypertension are if that is their case, to avoid unnecessary worry.

#### I.5.2 The information gap

A lack of information can be a source of anxiety and uncertainty. Not understanding clinical systems, being unable to formulate pertinent questions and feeling undervalued in clinical consultations are all common experiences for patients, which exacerbate the information gap. In contrast, the presence of information can enable engagement in self- care and can support changes in lifestyle which result in a more effective management of glaucoma.

Key information gaps include:

* **Nature of glaucoma sight loss**
  
  Even long-term patients may struggle to understand the nature of glaucoma sight loss. Helping people to understand the specifics of their own field loss can also help them develop techniques to avoid trips and falls. People may assume that surgery or laser will improve vision, so volunteering the correct information is often helpful.

* **Glaucoma and driving**
  
  This is one of the major sources of stress and anxiety for patients, yet there can be confusion about local driving regulations and when a patient may need to notify the authorities. This anxiety is understandable given the potential impact of losing a driving license.

* **Eye drops**
  
  Patients’ ability to manage their condition varies depending on their personal circumstances. Drops change, personal circumstances change, attitudes to treatment evolve. Continue checking in with your patients, encourage discussion and frame questions to avoid judgement or censure. E.g. “Do you have any concerns or difficulties with your eye drops”?
  
  Education on eye drop administration is part of the clinical approach. Patients need ongoing information about adherence- not only when their drop regimen changes or when there are supply issues or side effects. Patients need to be encouraged to speak up when they have problems with their drops, and need to know whom to ask for help.

* **Surgery and laser treatment**
  
  The route to making a treatment decision is complex, and many patients need considerable support, advice and time. The possible outcomes and risks of their condition and of the treatment are to be explained in a manner suitable to each individual. Eye surgery is a routine part of our work, but it can sound terrifying for a patient. Providing accurate timely written information for people to take away can mean patients are reassured and empowered to decide and understand the pros and cons of the procedure.

* **Asking questions is difficult**
  
  Patients often find it hard to ask for information from healthcare professionals. Some find the clinical setting is not conducive to engagement, others describe doctors who don’t want to engage with them, and many ration their time with their healthcare provider because they feel guilty about using doctors’ time. For others, the obstacle lies in not knowing how to frame questions about their glaucoma due to lack of knowledge or difficulties with memory or hearing that inhibits people.
  
  Clinicians should help by inviting questions at every single appointment, encouraging patients to bring written questions with them, or to take along a friend or relative for support.

* **Glaucoma support groups**
  
  These are excellent vehicles for the dissemination of information from a patient’s perspective which offer valuable peer support opportunities. Give patients details of local or national support groups, where available, including suggestions about updated and reputable patient information links. Not everyone has access to the internet and if your clinic does not have printed material about glaucoma on hand, perhaps this could be obtained from other organizations.

In summary, patients’ information needs are complex – and equally complex for those newly diagnosed as for those diagnosed decades ago. Even patients who appear well focused may lack key information or skills to manage their condition. The healthcare professionals need to be proactive in encouraging questions and providing answers.

#### I.5.3 Tips for doctors

Here is a summary of the top tips presented by the Experts by Experience Committee (a panel of glaucomatous patients) at the Dublin 2024 European Glaucoma Society Congress:

* 1) Explain to the patient what glaucoma is and its effect on the eyes – please don’t assume it is known.
  
  Explain in simple everyday terms as far as possible and ensure the patient has understood what you’re saying before they leave your clinic. Include the form of glaucoma they have and their choices for treatment.
* 2) Make suggestions you feel are relevant for this patient as to how to live with glaucoma. Let them know about any assistance they could get.
* 3) Explain well the importance of medical treatment to control eye pressure, and ensure the patient understands that taking the drops and using correct administration techniques will limit further damage, but will not improve vision.
* 4) Explain clearly how and when to administer eye drops.
  
  Mention dry eye problems, preservative-free drugs and the possible need to change eye drops over time.
* 5) Explain the pros and cons of any surgical treatment suggested, including side- effects.
  
  Also talk about alternative treatments. While prescribing medications provide details regarding the time to administer the specific medication.
* 6) Address the possible interactions between glaucoma and other health issues the patient may have, including pregnancy for women.
* 7) Motivate the patient to inform their environment at work and among their circle of friends about their condition.
  
  Explain how to tell family members, who also might inherit the disease. If a child has glaucoma, allow extra time to talk to family.
* 8) Inform patients that there are patient organisations, support groups and other good sources of information about glaucoma and how to live with it.

#### I.5.4 Key points for healthcare providers working with paediatric glaucoma patients

Paediatric glaucoma requires a nuanced approach that combines clinical expertise with a deep understanding of the psychosocial and developmental needs of the child and their caregivers. Doctors should prioritize clear communication, empathetic care, and tailored strategies that address both medical and emotional challenges within the time constraints of clinical practice. Caring for these high demand patients usually is usually done in tertiary centres that have enough volume and expertise. This would provide clinical experience but also a setup that has the required multidisciplinary team to support both child and caregivers.

##### I.5.4.1 Comprehensive Assessment: Understanding the Whole Picture

Begin with a thorough medical and family history to identify genetic predispositions, consanguinity of parents, associated systemic conditions (e.g., Sturge-Weber syndrome, Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome), and risk factors such as corticosteroid use or ocular trauma. Use age-appropriate assessments to evaluate the child’s visual function and developmental impact, asking caregivers about daily challenges and milestones:

Encourage caregivers to share their observations, which often provide valuable insight into the child’s condition and adaptation. Caregivers often experience profound anxiety and grief when their child is diagnosed with glaucoma. Interaction with the patient will depend on the patient’s age and maturity. Questions can range from social interaction to ability to perform activities in school, among others.

Paediatric glaucoma management often involves a multidisciplinary team. Facilitate access to resources such as vision therapy and mobility training, educational support for children with visual impairments or peer support groups for caregivers to share experiences and strategies and reducing feelings of isolation. Provide caregivers with contact information for national organizations or local resources that can assist with their journey.

Examples of questions to both caregivers and patients:

_“How is your child managing tasks like recognizing faces or navigating familiar spaces?” “Are there activities they are struggling with due to their vision?”_

_“How is the child doing at school?”_

_“Have you noticed any behavioural changes recently?”_

_“Do you feel your vision affects your ability to see the board or play sports?”_

### I.6 Glaucoma epidemiology

Glaucoma is a leading cause of vision impairment and is globally the most common cause of irreversible blindness. 1,2 Early epidemiological studies focused on predominantly Caucasian populations in higher income countries. More recent population-based studies have provided data for broader regions which have enabled more accurate modelling of the prevalence and morbidity of the disease. 3-9 As more countries undergo their epidemiological transition, ¹⁰ the burden of glaucoma worldwide is likely to increase significantly over the coming decades. This will require significant development of resources and technology to ensure healthcare access for all those that require it. Several ocular and systemic risk factors have been well established for glaucoma. Future research may help elucidate additional risk factors and enable a more precise quantification of the relative contribution of each to glaucoma susceptibility. Furthermore, advances in the genetic characterization of glaucoma may enhance the accuracy of individualized risk stratification.

#### I.6.1 Burden of glaucoma

The most prevalent form of glaucoma is primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) with an estimated global prevalence in adults aged 40 to 80 years of 3.05% (95% l, 1.69-5.27). ¹¹ Using data from 14 population based studies, 2.99% (12.3 million) of the European population aged 40+ years are estimated to have glaucoma, and more than half (56.4%) of cases undiagnosed. ¹² Conversely, there are very limited data on the overdiagnosis and overtreatment of POAG, which is also expected to occur in clinical practice. The Thessaloniki Eye Study reported that the overdiagnosis of POAG is substantial in an elderly white European population. ¹³ By 2050, one further million cases are anticipated in Europe due to aging population. ¹²

Glaucoma is estimated to be responsible for between 11-14% of all cases of blindness, globally 1,2 and 26% of those blind indifiduals are in high income countries. ² In 2020, 279,000, 1,350,000 and 681,000 people were estimated blind due to glaucoma in Central, Western and Eastern Europe, respectively. Subjects with visual impairment by glaucoma in these regions numbered 3,269,000, 11,055,000 and 8,943,000, respectively. Between years 2000 and 2020, age-standardised prevalence of glaucoma blindness decreased in Central, Western and Eastern Europe, by 14%, 11% and 26%, respectively, while decreases in moderate and severe vision impairment were more modest (2%; 1%; 2%). ¹

#### I.6.2 Natural history of glaucoma and blindness

While OAG is far more common than ACG, blindness is more likely to happen in ACG than in OAG (estimated 25% and 10% over the patient lifetime, respectively). Due to the established benefit of IOP-lowering treatment in glaucoma, there have been very few opportunitities to study the course of untreated glaucoma over time. Valuable data on the natural course of OAG have also been provided by the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT, see 1.7.1.3), the United Kingdom Glaucoma Treatment Study

(UKGTS, see 1.7.1.5) and the Collaborative Normal-Tension Glaucoma Study (CNTGS, see 1.7.1.1). In the untreated arm of the EMGT, the overall natural rate of progression in the VF was 1.08 dB/year. Participants with different disease phenotypes exhibited different rates of progression (1.31 dB/year in high tension glaucoma, 0.36 dB/year in normal tension glaucoma and 3.13 dB/year in pseudoexfoliative glaucoma (PXFG). ²¹ See Fig. I.6.2 .

#### I.6.3 Risk factors for glaucoma

Several risk factors for glaucoma have been long established with age and IOP remaining the most significant. 11 21 Non-White ethnicity (particularly Black), family history of glaucoma, pseudoexfoliation, disc haemorrhage, thinner cornea and myopia have been reported as major risk factors for the development and/or progression of OAG. 22-24 The highest prevalence of PACG appears in East-Asian and Chinese ethnicities. ¹¹

There is continuing research into further ocular and systemic risk factors for glaucoma with an aim to provide the most accurate risk stratification tools for clinicians. There has been significant interest in corneal biomechanical properties in recent years, although the pathophysiological mechanism by which they increase glaucoma risk remains unclear. Further investigations into systemic risk factors continues. Studies have often found conflicting evidence regarding these, for example with diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnoea.

There is increasing evidence supporting the role of blood pressure. In particular, several prevalence and incidence studies reported that low diastolic blood pressure is associated with increased risk for glaucoma. Some of those studies revealed a potential role of antihypertensive treatment in combination with lowered diastolic blood pressure. 25-26

#### I.6.4 The future of glaucoma management and policy implications

As more countries worldwide experience an epidemiological transition towards increasing mean age the number of patients with glaucoma will significantly rise over the coming decades. Regions with the highest prevalence of glaucoma often have the most limited healthcare resources. To meet this growing demand there will need to be efficient utility of resources, improved access to care, and improved awareness of the disease. ²⁵ This will require adequate workforce planning globally to provide the ophthalmologists and non-ophthalmologist healthcare professionals to care for these patients.

Technologies which enable remote consultation and monitoring may alleviate shortages of healthcare professionals. With greater refinement, mobile applications which enable the home assessment of visual acuity and visual field may enable a large degree of home monitoring. Furthermore, the development of screening programmes may help target healthcare resources to those with greatest need and greater risk.

Ongoing research into ocular and systemic risk factors may help develop a significantly improved degree of individual risk stratification in the future. Finally, further understanding of the genetics of the condition may significantly increase our ability to determine individual risk and response to therapies as glaucoma management enters the age of personalised medicine. See Ch I.5 and I.6 .

* **Thanks to many recent well-conducted population-based studies in Europe we now have a much better understanding of glaucoma prevalence and underdiagnosis, which cannot be captured with studies based on hospital/ clinic/volunteers.**
* **Age-standardised prevalence of glaucoma blindness and vision impairment has decreased over the last 20 years in Europe. Although this is to be welcomed, the epidemiological transition, that includes changing age structure, means that glaucoma cases will continue to increase.**
* **Meeting current and future needs requires the efficient use of resources, enhanced access to care, greater disease awareness, and the adoption of personalized medicine.**

#### I.7.1 Treatment vs no treatment trials in open angle glaucoma

##### I.7.1.1 Collaborative normal tension glaucoma study (CNTGS)

The CNTGS compared treatment versus no treatment in normal tension glaucoma in a multi-centre, randomised trial. 230 eligible patients entered the study. Only those who exhibited verified progression of visual field (VF) loss or threat to fixation were randomised (n=140). The primary outcome measure was disease progression as evident from VF or stereo disc photographs. ¹

Summary of results : 2-5

* – A 30% intraocular pressure (IOP) reduction from baseline was the treatment goal and was maintained in nearly 50% of patients. Progression occurred in 12% (7/61) of treated eyes and 35% (28/79) of controls.
* – In the intent-to-treat analysis no benefit of treatment was found.
* – A beneficial effect of IOP lowering was found only after the data were censored for the effect of cataract formation on the VF.
* – Cataracts were more common in patients treated with surgery.
* – Progression rates varied widely. The mean rate of worsening was 0.41 dB/year in the untreated arm. Prior documented progression did not increase the risk of future progression.

##### I.7.1.2 The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS)

The OHTS was a multicentre, randomised, clinical trial, designed to study the effect of topical medication in delaying or preventing the onset of glaucoma in patients with ocular hypertension (OHT). A total of 1636 patients were recruited. Randomisation was between treatment with medications and no treatment. The treatment goal was to lower the IOP to less than 24 mmHg and at least 20% from baseline. The primary outcome was the development of primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) defined as reproducible VF defects or reproducible optic disc deterioration. After the 5-year initial results were reported the control group received treatment. ¹

Summary of results : 2-6

* – Mean IOP reduction was 22.5% in the treated group. The control group showed a decrease of IOP of 4.0%.
* – After 5 years, 4.4% of patients in the treated group had developed signs of glaucoma damage versus 9.5% in controls (p < 0.0001), a 50% reduction of relative risk.
* – In addition, more than 90% of untreated patients had not converted to glaucoma after 5 years.
* – After 13 years (OHTS-II) 22% of patients who had initially been randomised to the control group with no treatment and received treatment after a median of 7.5 years, had converted to glaucoma versus 16% in the group that was treated at the start of the study. However, delaying treatment did not result in higher rates of conversion to glaucoma except in patients presenting with a higher baseline risk for conversion exceeding 13%.
* – POAG conversion was detected first in disc photographs in around 50% of patients and by field testing in approximately 40%.
* – Risk factors for development of glaucoma were: thinner CCT, higher IOP, disc haemorrhages, older age, larger vertical and horizontal CDR, greater VF pattern standard deviation (PSD).
* – Disc haemorrhages detectable in photographs had been missed at 87% of clinical examinations. Rate of conversion was higher in eyes with haemorrhages.
* – A risk calculator is freely available to estimate the risk of developing glaucoma at 5 years. _<https://ohts.wustl.edu/risk/>_
* – Cataract formation was more common in the medication group.
* – Collectively, analysis of VF data from OHTS studies revealed that some patients may experience more rapid progression than others. ⁸

##### I.7.1.3 The Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT)

The EMGT was a randomised, prospective trial comparing treatment versus no treatment to evaluate the effectiveness of IOP reduction in early, previously untreated open angle glaucoma. ¹ Secondary aims were to assess factors related to glaucoma progression and to determine the natural history of the disease.

During a population-based screening among 44,243 residents in Sweden, 316 eyes of 255 patients were recruited between 1993 and 1997, and followed prospectively until December 31, 2013. Treated patients received a standardised treatment protocol of laser trabeculoplasty and topical betaxolol. Treatment or no-treatment remained unchanged as long as definite progression had not occurred. Primary outcome measure was progression of disease, defined by sustained VF deterioration or optic disc changes.

Summary of results : 2-18

* – This study was the first to prove and quantify the value of IOP reduction in patients with POAG, normal tension glaucoma (NTG) and pseudoexfoliative glaucoma (PXFG).
* – A 25% decrease in IOP from baseline (mean untreated IOP 20.6 mmHg) reduced the relative risk of progression by 50%.
* – Risk of progression was smaller with lower baseline IOP values and with a larger initial IOP drop induced by treatment.
* – Treatment efficacy in terms of IOP reduction depended very much on pre-treatment IOP.
* – Important risk factors for progression were: higher IOP, pseudoexfoliative syndrome (PXF), more baseline damage, higher age, disc haemorrhages, thinner CCT in high tension glaucoma, and low blood pressure in NTG.
* – IOP fluctuation was not a risk factor for progression.
* – IOP did not increase but remained constant over time in untreated eyes with POAG but increased over time in eyes with PXFG.
* – Increase in lens opacity occurred more in the treatment arm than in the control arm.
* – There was no evidence of VF improvement on initiation of glaucoma therapy.
* – Disease progression rates varied substantially between individual patients.
* – Untreated progression rates (natural history) were slower in NTG (-0.36 dB/year), faster in high tension glaucoma (-1.31 dB/year), and even faster in eyes with PXFG (-3.10 dB/year).
* – Definite progression was associated with a mean worsening of mean defect (MD) of less than 2dB.
* – In eyes with manifest glaucoma, progression in the VF was detected first more than 4 times as often as progression in the optic disc. Among fellow eyes without VF loss at baseline, progression was detected first as frequently in the optic disc as in the VF. Perimetric progression was detected first at all stages of the disease.
* – After a few years of follow-up, vision-related quality of life (QoL) did not differ between treatment arms, i.e. the absence or presence of treatment did not influence QoL. An analysis after 20 years of follow-up supports the widespread, albeit arbitrary, use of a better-eye remaining VFI loss greater than 50% or MD worse than -18 dB as an important threshold for a significant reduction in vision-related QoL.
* – The frequency of disc haemorrhages was higher with lower IOP, in women and with myopia and was not influenced by treatment.
* – An analysis of EMGT patients followed for at least 15 years showed that a glaucoma diagnosis made by applying strict criteria to 2 initial VF tests, supported by optic disc findings if VF findings were borderline, was almost always correct.

##### I.7.1.4 European Glaucoma Prevention Study (EGPS)

The EGPS was a multicentre, randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled clinical trial. The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of IOP reduction with dorzolamide in preventing glaucoma damage in patients with OHT. The patients were randomised into 2 groups: active therapy (topical dorzolamide) and placebo. Main outcome measures were VF and/or optic disc changes. ¹

Summary of results : 2-6

* – 1081 patients were enrolled. The median duration of follow-up was 55 months.
* – The IOP difference between the treatment and the control group was small. The mean IOP reduction was 15% after 6 months and 22% after 5 years in the dorzolamide group, but there was also a 9% reduction after 6 months and 19% after 5 years in the placebo group, to a large part attributable to high attrition.
* – The study failed to detect a statistically significant difference between the chosen medical therapy and placebo, either in IOP lowering effect, or in the rate of progression to POAG, and attrition was large.
* – The same predictors for the development of POAG were identified independently in both the OHTS observation group and the EGPS placebo group: baseline older age, higher IOP, thinner central corneal thickness (CCT), larger vertical cup/disc ratio (CDR), and higher Humphrey VF PSD. Diuretics use was pointed as a possible risk factor.
* – In a later paper, several baseline Heidelberg retina tomograph (HRT) parameters, alone or in combination with baseline clinical and demographic factors, were significantly associated with the development of open angle glaucoma among the EGPS participants.

##### I.7.1.5 United Kingdom Glaucoma Treatment Study (UKGTS)

The UKGTS was a multicentre, randomised, masked, placebo-controlled trial designed to assess visual function preservation in open angle glaucoma (OAG) patients given latanoprost 0.005% compared with those given placebo. 516 individuals were enrolled. The primary outcome was time to VF deterioration within 24 months. Progression was measurable within such a time frame since the frequency of VF examination was increased. This placebo-controlled trial is the only one to quantify VF preservation with a single IOP-lowering drug in patients with OAG, in this case a prostaglandin. ¹

Summary of results : 2-6

* – Untreated IOP was 19.6 ± 4.6 mmHg and 20.1 ± 4.8 mmHg in the latanoprost group and in the placebo group, respectively.
* – Mean reduction in IOP was 3.8 ± 4.0 mmHg in the latanoprost group and 0.9 ± 3.8 mmHg in the placebo group.
* – 25.6% patients in the placebo group reached the VF deterioration endpoint at 24 months compared with 15.2% in the latanoprost group.
* – The 20% reduction in IOP in the latanoprost group, from a baseline of 19.6 mmHg, was associated with significantly longer VF preservation than in the placebo group (HR: 0.44).
* – The risk of progression increased by 7% per mmHg higher baseline IOP, by 59% if both eyes of a patient had glaucoma, and was double if baseline disc haemorrhage was present.
* – Patient age, severity of VF loss, and IOP fluctuations were not associated with risk of progression.
* – QoL was not different between treatment arms. The Patient Reported Outcomes (PROM’s) used were not sensitive enough to function as primary endpoints for this trial.
* – Faster rates of retinal nerve fibre layer thinning, measured by optical coherence tomography (OCT), was associated with a greater risk of VF progression.
* – VF change in the first 3 months was no different between treatment and placebo arms.
* – Combining VF and OCT data identified progression more quickly than using only VF data.

#### I.7.2 Treatment vs no treatment trials on angle closure

##### I.7.2.1 Zhongshan Angle Closure Prevention study (ZAP)

The ZAP was a single-centre, randomised controlled trial designed to evaluate the efficacy of laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) in preventing primary angle closure (PAC) or acute angle closure (AAC), in primary angle closure suspects (PACS). After a population-based screening involving 11991 participants, 889 untreated Chinese PACS, defined as irido- trabecular contact of at least 180 degrees without peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) or raised IOP, were enrolled. One eye of each participant was randomly assigned to receive LPI with the fellow eye left untreated. The primary outcome was incident PAC disease, as a composite of three endpoints, including PAS or IOP over 24 mmHg or AAC. ¹

Summary of the results : 2-6

* – Overall, there was a difference between treatment groups but the frequency of patients reaching the primary outcome was very low.
* – At 6 years, primary outcome event occurred in 19 treated eyes (4.19 per 1000 eye- years) and 36 untreated eyes (7.97 per 1000 eye-years) (p=0.0041).
* – At 14-years extended follow up, a primary endpoint occurred in 33 LPI-treated eyes (4.27 per 1000 eye-years) and 105 control eyes (13.59 per 1000 eye-years) (p<0.001).
* – LPI was associated with 47% and 69% reduction of relative risk of PAC or AAC after 6 years (HR 0.53) and 14 years (HR 0.31), respectively.
* – One of the LPI-treated eyes developed an acute attack of angle closure whereas 5 did so in control eyes.
* – In untreated eyes the risk of PAC occurrence was associated with higher IOP, shallower limbal anterior chamber depth, smaller central anterior chamber depth and narrower angle width measured by Anterior Segment OCT.
* – It is uncertain whether the findings of this trial are generalisable to non-Chinese populations. In addition, patients recruited in ZAP-trial were asymptomatic, did not have cataracts and had on average deeper anterior chambers depth, compared with patients treated with LPI in clinics.
* – The authors suggested that prophylactic LPI should not be performed routinely in PACS. LPI is advisable only in high-risk eyes. In general PACS patients encountered at tertiary referral centres may represent more advanced cases with respect to ocular biometrics parameters and may be at higher risk compared to ZAP trial participants.

##### I.7.2.2 The Singapore asymptomatic narrow angles laser iridotomy study (ANA-LIS)

The ANA-LIS Study was an open-label, paired-eye, randomised controlled trial investigating prophylactic LPI versus no treatment in PACS. 480 participants (mostly women and Chinese) with bilateral PACS, defined as irido-trabecular contact of at least 180 degrees without PAS or raised IOP, were randomised to receive LPI in one eye and no treatment in the fellow eye. Summary of results : 1-2

* – No differences were seen in IOP and in the development of PACG.
* – Older age and higher IOP after dilatation were associated with an increased risk of an end point developing.
* – The overall progression rate from PACS to PAC or POAG was low, and the authors suggested that observation without LPI is a reasonable option for PACS.

#### I.7.3 Studies comparing treatment in open angle glaucoma

##### I.7.3.1 Advanced Glaucoma Intervention Study (AGIS)

AGIS was a multicentre, prospective randomised study in patients with OAG who could not be controlled by maximally-tolerated medical therapy alone. 591 patients (789 eyes) were randomised between two sequences of treatments.

1. ATT: argon laser trabeculectomy (ALT), followed by trabeculectomy, followed by a second trabeculectomy, or
2. TAT: trabeculectomy, followed by ALT, followed by a second trabeculectomy.

The surgical technique for performing trabeculectomies changed during the study period.

Prior to 1990, antimetabolites were not used during surgery. After 1990, 5-Fluorouracil was used postoperatively. After 1991, mitomycin-C was used intraoperatively. Enrolled eyes had consistent elevation of IOP of ≥ 18 mmHg. Patients with MD worse than -16 dB were excluded, thus excluding eyes with very advanced glaucoma. About 1/3 of patients had early glaucoma. The main outcomes of interest were decreased VF or visual acuity. ¹

Summary of results : 2-9

* – After 7 years, mean reduction of IOP was greater for eyes assigned to the TAT protocol, and the cumulative probability of failure of the first intervention was greater for eyes assigned to the ATT protocol.
* – The percentage of eyes with decreased visual acuity or VF progression was lower for the ATT sequence than for TAT in African American patients. Initial trabeculectomy slowed the progression of glaucoma more effectively in patients with white European ancestry.
* – The probability of cataract formation after 5 years was high after trabeculectomy, 78%.
* – Risk factors associated with progression were older age, longer follow-up, and increasing number of glaucoma interventions.
* – IOP fluctuations were a risk factor for VF progression only in patients with mean IOP at low teens.
* – Both ALT and trabeculectomy failed more often in younger patients and in eyes with higher pre-treatment IOP.
* – In a post-hoc analysis of patients with 6-years of follow-up or more, eyes with an average IOP>17.5 mmHg over the first three 6-months visits showed more frequent VF deterioration compared to eyes with an average IOP<14 mmHg.
* – Eyes with IOP<18 mmHg at 100% of the visits experienced no mean MD progression, whereas eyes with less stringent IOP control demonstrated VF progression.

##### I.7.3.2 Collaborative Initial Glaucoma Treatment Study (CIGTS)

The CIGTS was a multicentre randomised controlled trial aimed at finding out if newly diagnosed OAG is better treated by initial treatment with medications or by immediate filtration surgery.1 A total of 607 patients with newly diagnosed OAG were randomised to initial treatment with either medication or trabeculectomy (with or without 5-fluorouracil). A target IOP algorithm was used tailored for each individual eye. Primary outcome variables were VF progression and QoL. Secondary outcome variables were visual acuity, IOP, and cataract formation. Inclusion criteria may have allowed recruitment of some patients with OHT, resulting in a case mix with a smaller risk of showing progression, patients with severe OAG were excluded. ¹

Summary of results : 2-10

* – IOP reduction was larger with surgery (48%; mean post treatment IOP 14-15 mmHg) than with medications (35%; mean post treatment IOP 17-18 mmHg).
* – In the first few years, mean perimetric progression among all subjects was small and similar in both groups. After 8 years, 21% of surgical patients and 25% of medical patients had progressed, defined as a worsening of MD by 3 dBs.
* – After adjustment for baseline risk factors, larger IOP variation measures were associated with significantly worse MD values after 3 to 9 years in the medication arm but not in the surgically treated group.
* – QoL was initially better in the medically treated group but there was no difference in QoL at the last follow-up. Worry about becoming blind was reported by 50% of CIGTS participants at baseline but decreased in both treatment groups to 25% and remained constant thereafter.
* – Patients randomised to the surgery arm underwent cataract surgery more than twice as often as patients in the medical treatment group.
* – Reversal of optic disc cupping was seen in 13% in the surgical group but was not associated with improved visual function.
* – 1.1% of surgical patients had developed endophthalmitis after 5 years.
* – Risk factors for progression included higher baseline IOP, worse baseline VF status, and lower level of education.
* – Risk factors for progression differed by treatment group. Patients with more advanced VF loss at baseline had less risk of progression when they received initial surgery versus medication but VF progression among participants with diabetes who received surgery was greater than those receiving medication. Greater VF progression was observed among medication arm participants who reported poorer adherence to medications.

##### I.7.3.3 Low-Pressure Glaucoma Treatment Study (LoGTS)

The Low-Pressure Glaucoma Treatment Study (LoGTS) was a randomised, multicentre, double-masked trial comparing visual field (VF) stability in low-pressure glaucoma patients treated with twice-daily brimonidine tartrate 0.2% vs. timolol maleate 0.5%.

Eligible patients were ≥30 years old with untreated IOP ≤21 mmHg and no advanced VF loss or medication contraindications. Both eyes were randomised to monotherapy. Follow-up included Humphrey 24-2 perimetry, tonometry every 4 months, and annual optic disc photos.

Main outcome measure was VF progression in either eye, defined by ≥3 points with a negative slope ≥-1 dB/year at p<5% on 3 consecutive tests (pointwise linear regression). Secondary outcome measures were progression based on glaucoma change probability maps (GCPM) of pattern deviation and the 3-omitting method for pointwise linear regression.

A total of 99 patients received brimonidine and 79 received timolol. Mean follow-up was 30.0 ± 2 months. Of 190 enrolled, 12 (6.3%) were excluded post-randomization and 77 (40.5%) did not complete 4 years. ¹

Summary of the results :

* – Statistically fewer brimonidine-treated patients (9.1%) had visual field progression by pointwise linear regression than timolol-treated patients (39.2%, p=0.001).
* – Eyes randomised to timolol progressed faster (mean rates of progression, -0.38 ± 0.9 vs 0.02 ± 0.7 dB/y, p <0 .01).
* – Older age (HR = 1.41/decade older, p = .022), use of systemic antihypertensives HR = 2.53, p = .005), and mean ocular perfusion pressure (HR = 1.21/mm Hg lower, p < .001) were associated with progression whereas randomization to brimonidine revealed a protective effect (HR = 0.26,, p < .001).
* – Mean treated IOP was similar across groups at all time points.
* – Mean deviation and corrected pattern standard deviation from the visual fields were not correlated with Imean, peak, trough, or peak minus trough IOPs.
* – In unilateral VF loss cases (n = 53, there were no differences in any IOP parameter between eyes.
* – More brimonidine patients discontinued due to adverse events (28.3% vs. 11.4%, p = 0.008).
* – Due to the lack of data from the 12 excluded participants and the 77 who did not complete follow-up, no definitive conclusions can be made regarding potential IOP-independent effects of brimonidine.

##### I.7.3.4 The Tube versus Trabeculectomy Study (TVT)

The TVT Study enrolled 212 eyes from 212 patients at 17 centres—107 in the tube group and 105 in the trabeculectomy group. The mean age was 71 years, and 53% were female. Baseline intraocular pressure (IOP) was 25.3 ± 5.3 mm Hg, with 81% diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma.

Eligible participants were aged 18–85 with prior trabeculectomy and/or cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation, and uncontrolled glaucoma (IOP 18–40 mm Hg) on maximally tolerated medical therapy. Qualifying prior surgeries included cataract extraction (44%), trabeculectomy (35%), and combined procedures (20%).

Patients were randomised to receive either a 350 mm ² Baerveldt glaucoma implant or trabeculectomy with mitomycin C (0.4 mg/mL for 4 minutes). Scheduled follow-ups occurred at 1 day, 1 week, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months, then annually through 5 years. Failure was defined prospectively as IOP >21 mm Hg or <20% reduction from baseline on two consecutive visits after 3 months, IOP ≤5 mm Hg on two visits after 3 months, reoperation for glaucoma, or loss of light perception.

Summary of results : 2-9

* – Mean IOP was significantly lower in the trabeculectomy group during the first 3 months, but no sustained differences were observed thereafter.
* – The tube group required more medications during the first 2 years. Over time, medication use increased in the trabeculectomy group, equalizing between groups by year 3.
* – At 5 years, cumulative failure rates were 29.8% (tube) and 46.9% (trabeculectomy) (p = 0.002; HR 2.15; 95% CI: 1.30–3.56).
* – Post hoc analyses using stricter IOP thresholds showed higher failure in the trabeculectomy group:
  
    + ≤17 mm Hg: 31.8% (tube) vs. 53.6% (trabeculectomy) (p = 0.002; HR 2.04)
    + ≤14 mm Hg: 52.3% vs. 71.5%, respectively (p = 0.017; HR 1.57)
* – Postoperative complications were more frequent in the trabeculectomy group (63% vs. 43%, p = 0.006), though most were transient. The incidence of serious complications (requiring reoperation or causing ≥2-line Snellen VA loss) was similar between groups (22% tube vs. 20% trabeculectomy, p = 0.79).

##### I.7.3.5 Treatment of Advanced Glaucoma Study (TAGS)

The TAGS was a pragmatic, multicentre, randomised controlled trial designed to evaluate the best primary therapeutic approach in advanced glaucoma. A total of 453 patients with newly diagnosed untreated severe OAG glaucoma (based on Hodapp- Parrish-Anderson classification) were Randomised 1:1 to initially receive one or more medication (primary medical treatment group) or MMC-augmented trabeculectomy (primary trabeculectomy group). Target IOP was individualized at baseline (based on Canadian Consensus on target IOP) and treatment could be escalated based on clinician’s judgment. The primary outcome was health-related QoL measured by VFQ-25. Secondary outcomes include IOP, VF MD, visual acuity, need for cataract surgery, PROMs by EQ-5D-5L, HUI-3. GUI, adverse events and health economic outcomes. Follow up was 2 years with a planned extension to 5 year. 1-2

Summary of results : 3-6

* – There were no differences for vision related QoL between groups. The mean ± SD VFQ-25 score in the medical treatment and trabeculectomy groups was 84.5 ± 16.3 and 85.4 ± 13.8, respectively at 2 years (p=0.38), 81.3 ± 17.5 and 83.3 ± 15.5 respectively at 5 years, (p=0.51).
* – No difference between groups were found for PROM’s as measured by EQ-5D-5L, HUI-3, and GUI.
* – IOP was consistently lower in the trabeculectomy group at all time points.
* – At 5 years IOP was 12.07 ± 5.18 mmHg in the trabeculectomy group and 14.76 ± 4.14 mmHg in the medical treatment group (p<0.001).
* – At 5 years mean VF MD was better in the trabeculectomy group (-14.30 ± 7.14) than the medical group (-16.74 ± 6.78) (p<0.001)
* – Visual acuity was worse in the trabeculectomy group at 2 years (mean difference 0.07; p=0.006) but no differences were found between groups at 5 years (mean difference 0.02; p=0.48). No unexplained loss of vision occurred immediately after surgery.
* – Fewer participants in the trabeculectomy group were receiving eye drops (35.4% vs 72.5% at 5 years).
* – Adverse events were similar between groups.
* – 8% of the trabeculectomy group did require an intervention to manage clinically significant hypotony.
* – Cost-effectiveness of trabeculectomy was worse at 24 months, but it has a higher probability of being cost effective over a patient’s lifetime.
* – The authors suggested that trabeculectomy can be offered as a primary intervention in advanced glaucoma.
