##### I.7.3.6 Glaucoma Intensive Treatment Study (GITS)

The GITS was a prospective, double-center, parallel group, open-label, Randomised trial to compare the efficacy of initial monotherapy versus intensive initial multitherapy in preserving visual function and QoL, in POAG and PXFG.

A total of 298 eyes of 242 newly diagnosed, untreated patients were randomised to receive either single-drug eye drop (monotherapy group) or a multi-treatment approach including 3 drugs, followed by a 360° laser trabeculoplasty (SLT or ALT) a week later (multitherapy group). According to VF progression, IOP or side-effects, treatment could be escalated or changed as needed. The primary outcome was the final VF status as assessed by three different criteria: the predicted VFI at the end of expected lifetime; the rate of progression of VF damage; a definite VF progression based on EMGT progression event analysis. Patients with VFI<65% were excluded. Follow up was 5 years.

Summary of results : 1-3

* – The projected VFI at predicted end of life, was 79.3% in the mono-treatment group and 87.1% in the multi-treatment group (p= 0.15).
* – The VFI median rate of progression was -0.66%/year in the monotherapy group and -0.25% in the multitherapy group, but this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.09).
* – Subgroup analysis of patients with higher baseline IOP (>24 mmHg) showed that the rate of progression was 5.5 times faster in the monotherapy group (p=0.06).
* – The number of participants reaching a definite VF progression event was higher in the monotherapy group (21% vs 11%) (p=0.03).
* – The median IOP over the 5 years of follow-up were 17 and 14 mmHg in mono- and in multitreatment groups.
* – Treatment was intensified in 49% of participants in the monotherapy group and in 12% of participants in the multitherapy group. 20 participants in the multitherapy group had treatment reduction. Six patients (5%) in the monotherapy group and 7 in the multitreatment group (6%) needed glaucoma surgery after treatment intensification.
* – Adverse events occurred in 25% of participants Randomised to monotherapy and 36% of those Randomised to multitherapy (p=0.04)
* – Authors concluded that initial intensive treatment may be considered in glaucoma patients with high untreated IOP at diagnosis. No evidence emerged about giving initial multitherapy routinely to all glaucoma patients.

##### I.7.3.7 Primary Tube versus Trabeculectomy Study (PTVT)

The PTVT Study was a multicentre, prospective, Randomised controlled trial comparing primary trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C (MMC) to tube shunt implantation (350 mm ² Baerveldt implant) in eyes with no history of prior incisional ocular surgery. A total of 242 eyes from 242 patients were enrolled across 16 clinical centres.

Eligible patients were 18–85 years old with IOP between 18–40 mm Hg on maximum tolerated medical therapy. The mean age was 61.4 ± 11.8 years, 66% were male, and 90% had primary open-angle glaucoma. The baseline IOP was 23.6 ± 5.3 mm Hg, and the mean number of medications was 3.2 ± 1.1. Patients were Randomised to receive either a tube shunt (Baerveldt 350 mm ² ) or trabeculectomy with MMC (0.4 mg/mL for 2 minutes). Follow-up visits occurred at 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and annually through 5 years. Failure was defined as IOP >21 mm Hg or <20% reduction from baseline on two consecutive visits after 3 months, IOP ≤5 mm Hg, reoperation for glaucoma, or loss of light perception. Complete success was defined as IOP control without medications, while qualified success allowed the use of medications.

Summary of the results :

* – At 1 year, the cumulative probability of failure was higher in the tube group (20%) than the trabeculectomy group (8%) (p = 0.02). At 3 years, failure remained higher in the tube group (39% vs 30%, p = 0.17), and at 5 years, the failure rate was 42% in the tube group vs 35% in the trabeculectomy group (p = 0.21; HR = 1.31; 95% CI = 0.86–2.01).
* – At 1 year, mean IOP was significantly lower in the trabeculectomy group (12.4 ± 4.4 mm Hg) than the tube group (13.8 ± 4.1 mm Hg, p = 0.01). This difference persisted at 3 years (12.1 ± 4.8 mm Hg vs 14.0 ± 4.2 mm Hg, p = 0.008), and at 5 years, IOP remained similar between groups (13.0 ± 5.2 mm Hg vs 13.4 ± 3.5 mm Hg, p = 0.52).
* – Baseline medication use was similar between groups. At 3 years, patients in the trabeculectomy group used fewer medications (1.2 ± 1.5) than those in the tube group (2.1 ± 1.4, p < 0.001). This difference persisted at 5 years (1.3 ± 1.4 vs 2.2 ± 1.3, p < 0.001).
* – At 1 year, complete success was more common in the trabeculectomy group (59% vs 14%, p < 0.001). At 3 years, complete success remained higher (44% vs 13%, p < 0.001). At 5 years, complete success was achieved in 34% of trabeculectomy patients vs 9% in the tube group. Qualified success at 5 years was 27% (trabeculectomy) vs 44% (tube).
* – Early (<1 month) complications occurred more frequently in the trabeculectomy group (33% vs 20%, p = 0.03). Late complications at 3 years were similar between groups (25% vs 22%, p = 0.65).

##### I.7.3.8 Laser in Glaucoma and Ocular Hypertension Trial (LiGHT)

The LiGHT was a multi-centre randomised controlled trial, comparing selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) versus eye-drops as first-line treatment for OHT or OAG.

A total of 718 newly diagnosed, untreated OHT or OAG patients were randomised to primary SLT, followed by topical medications as required (the SLT group), or topical medication (the drops group). Eyes in the SLT group, had up to two SLT treatments before drops if required. Target IOP, treatment escalation and monitoring intervals were individualized based on disease severity and pre-treatment IOP, and adjusted during the trial based on IOP control, disease stability and adverse reactions. The primary outcome was health-related QoL assessed with the EQ-5D. Secondary outcomes include glaucoma-specific be patients reported outcomes, clinical effectiveness, visual function and safety. Approximately 30% of study participants were OHT and 50% were early-stage OAG. Follow up was 3 years, extended to 6 years. ¹

Summary of results : 2-5

* – There were no differences in health-related QoL for the EQ-5D between the two groups.
* – 74.2% and 69.8% of the SLT group remained within target IOP without medication at 3 and 6 years of follow up, respectively.
* – Eyes in the SLT group required fewer trabeculectomies (nil vs 11) and suffered less disease progression than patients in the drops group (3.8% vs 5.8%) at 3 years. However, according to the study protocol patients in the SLT group were receiving medications in case more IOP lowering was needed, while patients in the drops group were not offered SLT but only trabeculectomy when more IOP lowering was needed.
* – After 6 years eyes in the SLT group underwent less trabeculectomy (2.4% vs 5.8%) (p<0.001) and less phacoemulsification (10.4 vs 17.3) (p=0.03), than eyes in the drops group.
* – At 6 years, 107 eyes (19.6%) in the SLT group showed disease progression compared with 147 eyes (26.8%) in the drops group (p=0.01).
* – A further analysis of total deviation of VF, confirmed that eyes initially treated with SLT showed slower VF progression than eyes with initial medical therapy.
* – SLT was safe and cost-effective compared with medications.
* – The authors suggested that SLT could be routinely offered as first line treatment to all newly diagnosed patients with OHT or POAG. It is uncertain whether the findings of this trial are generalizable to all stages of POAG, since the vast majority of study participants were either ocular hypertensives or had early stage damage.

#### I.7.4 Studies comparing treatment in angle closure

##### I.7.4.1 Effectiveness in Angle-closure Glaucoma of Lens Extraction Study (EAGLE)

The EAGLE study was a multicentre, randomised, prospective clinical trial designed to compare clear-lens extraction (CLE) vs LPI plus topical medical therapy as first line treatment in PAC or PACG. Eligible patients were aged 50 years or older, did not have cataracts, and had newly diagnosed PAC, with IOP 30 mmHg or greater, or PACG. A total of 419 patients were randomised to lens extraction (208, CLE group) or LPI (211, LPI group). Clinicians were allowed to escalate treatment to achieve target IOP. Primary outcome measures included QoL, assessed with the European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D), IOP, and cost-effectiveness, assessed at 3 years. ¹

Summary of results : 2-5

* – At 3 years, results show advantage of primary CLE over LPI for QoL and IOP.
* – Mean health status score on the EQ-5D (range 0; 1) after lens extraction was 0.052 higher than after LPI.
* – Mean IOP was 1.18 mm Hg lower after lens extraction than after LPI.
* – Significantly fewer participants in the CLE group needed medications (21% vs 61% with at least one drop) or glaucoma surgery (1 vs 24 operations) to control IOP.
* – Patients in the CLE group were 5 times more likely to have better long-term IOP control and 10 times more likely to be free of drops or surgery.
* – The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was better for initial CLE versus LPI (calculated on a subset of patients treated in the UK; not conclusive for other settings).
* – VF severity at 3 years remained similar in the two treatment groups.
* – This study supports the use of initial lens extraction as a first-line intervention for PAC with high IOP (≥ 30mmHg) or PACG, and in patients over 50 years of age. The study results are not generalisable to all PAC or PACG cases.
* – To note, in this trial the participating surgeons were experienced. Lens extraction to treat angle closure can be technically challenging.

Landmark clinical trials are studies considered as highly informative for patient management that clarified previously unclear answers to critical questions thus shaping paient care.

Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) are the highest level of evidence-based medicine and are pivotal for guiding clinical practice; however, results of a single RCT must be applied only to the same context of the study (i.e. clinical pathway, population enrolled, treatment options). Results of a RCT should be generalized with caution to patients different from those included in the trial.

### I.8 Cost-effectiveness of glaucoma care and glaucoma screening

#### I.8.1 Cost-effectiveness of glaucoma care

Cost-effectiveness is an important consideration when choosing diagnostic, monitoring and treatment interventions as well as when designing and evaluating glaucoma care pathways. Going forward, we need glaucoma studies to include measures of cost- effectiveness in their outcomes.

#### I.8.2 Screening for glaucoma

Screening for glaucoma has traditionally relied on case finding using costly and time- consuming diagnostic tools, which has made population-wide screening economically unviable and therefore not recommended to date. However, emerging technologies— such as artificial intelligence and genetic risk profiling through polygenic risk scores—hold promise to improve efficiency and reduce costs, potentially tipping the balance toward cost-effectiveness. While earlier economic models have yielded mixed conclusions, further research is needed to quantify the real-world benefits of population screening, particularly in preventing visual field loss, optic nerve damage, or declines in patient- reported outcomes.

#### I.8.3 Clinical and cost-effectiveness of diagnostic tests used for screening, detection and monitoring for glaucoma

Although there are numerous comparative diagnostic studies, there is no evidence regarding which combination of tests, or which testing frequency improve patient outcomes at a sustainable cost. Nevertheless, data from the UK suggests that a combination of structural tests may be cost-effective in triaging at-risk patients. Short follow-up intervals of less than 1 year for ocular hypertension or stable glaucoma are unlikely to be cost-effective.

There is a high degree of variability in the design and quality of diagnostic accuracy studies for glaucoma. When evaluating cost-effectiveness, it should be noted that care protocols and costs for patients and health systems vary hugely between different national and regional health systems. The cost of blindness should also be taken into consideration.

#### I.8.4 Cost-effectiveness of treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension preventing visual disability

Although direct evidence on the cost-effectiveness of glaucoma treatment is limited, hypotensive therapy remains a clinically justified approach due to its proven ability to slow disease progression and prevent vision loss.

Treatment of all OHT patients does not appear to be cost-effective. However, treatment of selected OHT patients with risk factors such as advanced age and higher pressures may be cost-effective in preventing conversion to glaucoma. On the other hand, it is not cost-effective to treat low-risk OHT individuals.

In glaucoma and OHT, evidence favors laser trabeculoplasty as the first-line treatment for glaucoma, because it may work better than topical medication in slowing down the VF progression at a lower cost compared to medications in some settings.

In advanced glaucoma, early trabeculectomy may be cost-effective when modelled over the patients’ life-time.

There are insufficient non-sponsored trials on MIGS to adequately evaluate the cost effectiveness of such procedures.

#### I.8.5 Cost-effectiveness research and glaucoma

So far, cost-effectiveness evaluation of glaucoma care pathways has been relatively unstructured, resulting in unclear and conflicting implications for clinical management. Future cost-effectiveness studies should include structured glaucoma-specific real- world data using electronic health records, also combining functional and structural measures. In addition, they should consider patients’ and clinicians’ perspectives, potential commercial bias, analysis of long-term outcomes, including direct and indirect costs and QoL measures, as well as tools to evaluate care pathway innovations and benchmark outcomes.

* While screening for OAG has not been shown to be cost-effective in the general population within high-resource settings, it may be cost-effective when targeted toward high-risk groups.
* Treatment of ocular hypertension is cost-effective only among OHT individuals with additional risk factors.
* In glaucoma and OHT, laser trabeculoplasty has shown to be cost-effective as first choice treatment.
* In advanced glaucoma, early trabeculectomy may be cost-effective when modelled over the patients’ life-time.
* In the future, we need glaucoma studies with outcomes that include measures of cost-effectiveness.

### I.9 Terminology, classification and definitions

Classification and disease definitions are necessarily arbitrary. A consensus can be reached only if they are acceptable to most ophthalmologists on both theoretical and practical grounds. There are conditions where a precise classification is particularly challenging, such as congenital disorders with associated anomalies.

The following features are to be considered in order to classify and manage the patient (see Fc II \- III ):

**Primary open angle glaucoma** is a chronic, progressive, potentially blinding, irreversible eye disease causing optic nerve rim and RNFL loss with related visual field defects. The angle is open with a normal appearance, and major risk factors include the level of IOP and older age. Visual disability is usually prevented by early diagnosis and treatment. See Ch II.2.2 .

#### II.1.1 Intraocular Pressure (IOP) and Tonometry

The intraocular pressure (IOP) in the population is approximately normally distributed with a curve skewed to the right. The mean IOP in adult populations is estimated at 15-16 mmHg, with a standard deviation of nearly 3.0 mmHg. Traditionally, the upper bound of normal IOP has been defined as two standard deviations above the mean, i.e. 21 mmHg, and any IOP above this level is considered to be elevated. However, any arbitrary threshold of IOP value alone will be unable to distinguish between health and disease. Higher IOP is a major risk factor for both the development of glaucoma and for its progression (see Ch II.3.3 and Fig II.3.2 ).

While IOP phasing may provide insights in certain cases, it is not routinely recommended due to its limited repeatability and weak correlation with disease progression. Nonetheless, measuring IOP at different times of the day can be beneficial in selected patients where clinical suspicion warrants closer monitoring.

##### II.1.1.1 Methods of measurement (tonometry)

Tonometry is based on the relationship between the IOP and the force necessary to deform the natural shape of the cornea by a given amount. Corneal biomechanical properties, such as thickness and elasticity, can affect the IOP measurements independently of the true IOP ( Table II.1.2 ). Tonometers can be classified as contact or non-contact. Some instruments are portable and hand-held.

To obtain reliable IOP measures, it is important to avoid Valsalva’s manoeuvre, breath- holding, squeezing the lids or the examiner touching the lids and pressing over the globe, all of which can lead to a momentary increase of the IOP. Furthermore, errors can be due to incorrect technique ( Fig. II.1.2 ) and to the biological variability of the cornea and eye.

###### II.1.1.1.1 Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT)

The GAT method involves illumination of a biprism tonometer head with a blue light (obtained using a cobalt filter). The prism is used to flatten the anaesthetised cornea which has fluorescein in the tear film. The scaled knob on the side of the instrument is then turned until the inner border of the two hemi-circles of fluorescent tear meniscus, visualised through each prism, just touch ( Fig. II.1.1 ).

The contact with the tear film and the cornea may raise concerns regarding transmissible disease when carrying out GAT. Chemical disinfection or the use of disposable tonometer heads is recommended. The tonometer calibration should be verified regularly according to the manufacturer instructions.

The Perkins tonometer is a portable version of GAT, usable also on supine patients. There has been substantial innovation in tonometry and newer methods (see next section) may challenge GAT’s current status as the reference standard.

###### II.1.1.1.2 Alternative Tonometers

A complete list of all available technologies is beyond the scope of the Guidelines.

Rebound tonometry

The rebound tonometer is portable and easy to use. Although it is a contact tonometer, topical anaesthetic drops are not required, and the tonometer has a disposable tip to minimise the risk of cross-infection. The device processes the rebound movement of a rod probe resulting from its interaction with the eye; rebound increases (shorter duration of impact) as the IOP increases. The rebound tonometer can be particularly useful in children and in adults with a small palpebral aperture or who cannot sit at a slit-lamp or chin-rest device. iCare is the most common rebound tonometer. With iCare, up to six measurements are taken and their average is displayed. A newer rebound tonometer is the Tono Vera which only takes readings when the device is perpendicularly aligned with the central cornea to avoid artefacts from off-centre readings. A version of rebound tonometry mounted at the slit lamp also exists. Rebound tonometry may be useful for patients with corneal disease and surface irregularity as the area of contact is small.

Ocular Response Analyser (ORA)

The ORA utilises air-puff technology to record two applanation measurements, one while the cornea is moving inward, and the other as the cornea returns towards its normal shape. The average of these two IOP values provides a Goldmann- correlated IOP measurement. The difference between these two IOP readings is called corneal hysteresis, a result of viscous dampening in the corneal tissue. The two applanation measurements provide a basis for two additional new parameters: corneal- compensated IOP (IOPcc) and corneal resistance factor. The corneal-compensated IOP is a measurement that is less affected by the corneal properties. The average of several good quality readings per eye is recommended.

Corvis ST tonometer

The Corvis ST is an air-puff tonometer combined with a high-speed Scheimpflug camera which records the corneal deformation during the air-puff. Outputs include an uncorrected IOP, a corneal biomechanically-corrected IOP and CCT.

The ORA and Corvis tonometers may be least affected by corneal biomechanical artefacts.

Non-contact tonometry (NCT)

The NCT or air-puff tonometry uses a rapid air pulse to flatten the cornea, thus working on the same basic principle as the Goldmann tonometer. The advantages include speed, no need for topical anaesthesia and no direct contact with the eye. NCT may overestimate the IOP in eyes with higher IOP. NCT is not recommended for monitoring glaucoma patients.

Dynamic contour tonometry (DCT)

This slit-lamp mounted instrument contains a sensor tip with a concave surface contour and a miniaturised pressure sensor. The result and a quality score measure are provided digitally. This technique may be less influenced by corneal properties

than GAT. The DCT additionally measures the ocular pulse amplitude which is the difference between the mean systolic and the mean diastolic IOP. The production of the Pascal DCT has been discontinued.

Tono-Pen

The Tono-Pen is a hand-held portable tonometer that determines IOP by making contact with the cornea (central contact is recommended) through a probe tip, causing applanation/indentation of a small area. Topical anaesthetic eye drops are used. After four or ten valid readings are obtained, depending on the instrument model, the averaged measurement is given together with the standard error.

###### II.1.1.1.3 Self Tonometry

Self-tonometry (e.g., with iCare Home) can be useful to better understand the longer-term level of IOP and variability in patients. Still in the research domain are surgically inserted intraocular IOP sensors which allow patients to easily measure their IOP by holding a receiver device near the eye.

###### II.1.1.1.4 Measurements in Supine position

Sometimes it is necessary to measure IOP in the supine position, e.g. bedside. Methods include certain versions of iCare, and also Perkins and Tonopen tonometers.

Many forms of tonometry have been licensed for clinical use through comparison with GAT, which is considered the current reference standard.

In general, all measurements with tonometers which applanate the cornea are influenced by corneal biomechanics. This concerns both geometries, e.g. thickness and curvature, and material properties, e.g. stiffness and viscoelasticity which play a role. The effect is greater with tonometers wich applanate the cornea more quickly, such as air-puff and rebound tonometers. The impact of tonometer inaccuracy and/or imprecision on clinical outcomes has not been established.

There is a sizeable inter-and intra-observer variability observed for all tonometers, including GAT.

The accuracy and precision of a tonometer should influence the choice for use in the clinic. For a given patient, the same type of tonometer should be used for follow-up.

##### II.1.1.2 Intraocular pressure and corneal thickness

Central corneal thickness (CCT) influences tonometry ( Table II.1.2 ). IOP correction algorithms based on CCT are not validated and are highly variable depending on the underlying population that was used to derive the correction coefficients. Therefore, applying a specific correction should be avoided. Rather, the CCT should guide a clinician as to whether there is likely an under- or over-estimation of IOP with their measurements. There are different methods to measure CCT. The normal distribution (mean ± SD) of ultrasonic CCT is approximately 540 ± 30 µm. The association between a thin CCT and a higher risk of glaucoma is likely due to its effect on IOP measurements rather than a true biological relationship with glaucoma pathogenesis. Therefore, CCT should not be used to assess risk of glaucoma in the general population, unless considered together with an IOP reading.

CCT variations after corneal refractive surgery make it difficult to interpret tonometric readings. A record of pre-operative CCT and IOP may be helpful to manage patients undergoing refractive surgery. Tonometers that aim to account for corneal biomechanical properties (see above) may be optimal for post-refractive surgery eyes. For example, the ORA IOPcc measure was optimised to minimise the difference in IOP before and after LASIK.

Corneal properties can have profound effects on IOP measurements. A growing number of patients have had corneal refractive surgery and while aging up to circa 2% are expected to develop glaucoma. Ophthalmologists should be aware that tonometry readings may substantially underestimate IOP in patients treated for the correction of myopia with corneal laser techniques. In such patients a correction using CCT values can only give indications. A tonometer device that aims to correct for dynamic corneal properties may be optimal, and careful monitoring of visual field and/or OCT in such glaucoma patients or suspects is required even with apparently low IOP.

CCT is one parameter which influences the accuracy of most tonometers. In eyes with thin corneas IOP tends to be underestimated and vice versa. Thinner CCT is associated with a higher risk of conversion of ocular hypertension (OHT) to glaucoma and a higher risk of glaucoma progression in multiple variable models. However, there is no strong evidence that CCT is an independent risk factor. IOP corrections based on CCT are not validated and should be avoided. (See I.3.2 Q.V.4 )

#### II.1.2 Gonioscopy

Gonioscopy is essential for evaluating patients suspected of having, or who have all types of glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

The purpose of gonioscopy is to inspect the anterior chamber angle. It is based on the recognition of angle landmarks and must always include an assessment of the following:

* Level of iris insertion, both apparent insertion without indentation and true insertion during indentation
* The shape of the peripheral iris profile, either flat, convex or concave
* Width of the iridocorneal angle between peripheral iris and cornea
* Degree, type and distribution of pigmentation in the trabecular meshwork
* Areas of iridotrabecular apposition or synechia
* Any abnormal or postoperative findings

##### II.1.2.1 Anatomy

###### II.1.2.1.1 Reference Landmarks

Schwalbe’s line : this collagen condensation of the Descemet’s membrane between the trabecular meshwork (TM) and the corneal endothelium appears as a thin translucent line. Schwalbe’s line may be prominent and anteriorly displaced (posterior embryotoxon), or there may be heavy pigmentation over it. A pigmented Schwalbe’s line (e.g. Sampaolesi’s line) may be misinterpreted as the TM, particularly when the iris is convex and the angle is narrow. The corneal wedge method is helpful to distinguish between the structures by reliably identifying Schwalbe’s line; this technique is particularly useful in cases of pale or poorly defined angle structures. Identifying Schwalbe’s line is a good starting point when performing gonioscopy (See Fig. II.1.3 ).

Trabecular Meshwork (TM) : extends posteriorly from Schwalbe’s line to the scleral spur. Close to Schwalbe’s line is the non-functional TM, which blends into the posterior, functional, and often pigmented TM. Most difficulties concerning the examination of the TM relate to determining whether observed features are normal o pathological (particularly pigmentation), blood vessels, and iris processes. Indentation (‘dynamic’) gonioscopy helps to visualise TM in angle closure (See Fig II.1.6 ).

Schlemm’s cana l: it is located anterior to the scleral spur, and it is not visible, though it may be seen if it contains blood. Blood reflux from episcleral veins may occur in cases of carotid-cavernous fistulae, Sturge Weber syndrome, venous compression, ocular hypotony, sickle cell disease or due to suction from the goniolens during gonioscopy.

Scleral spur : is of white appearance and located between the pigmented TM and the ciliary body. The angle is undoubtedly open if the scleral spur is visible. The scleral spur is a useful landmark in gonioscopy because it is relatively consistent in appearance and has less variability than other landmarks.

Ciliary band and iris root : the iris insertion is usually located at the anterior face of the ciliary body, though the site is variable. The ciliary band may be wide, as in myopia, aphakia or following trauma, or narrow or not seen as in hyperopia, angle closure and anterior insertion of the iris.

Pigmentation : pigment is found predominantly in the posterior TM. It is seen in adults, rarely before puberty and the extent can be highly variable. The most common conditions associated with dense pigmentation are PXF, pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS), previous trauma, previous laser treatment of the iris, uveitis and after angle- closure episodes. The inferior angle is usually the most open and pigmented. In older patients, the pigment reversal sign, where the trabecular meshwork appears darker in the superior quadrant than in the inferior quadrant is a sign suggesting previous PDS.

###### II.1.2.1.2 Other anatomical features

Blood vessels : these are often found in normal iridocorneal angles in subjects with blue/light irides. They characteristically have a radial or circumferential orientation, have few anastomoses and do not run across the scleral spur. Pathological vessels e.g., neovascularisation, are usually thinner, have a disordered orientation and run across the scleral spur. Abnormal vessels are also seen in Fuchs’ heterochromic iridocyclitis and chronic anterior uveitis.

Iris processes : are present in one-third of normal eyes and are more evident in younger subjects. When numerous and prominent, they may represent a form of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome/anomaly. They are distinguished from goniosynechiae, which are thicker and wider and may go beyond the scleral spur.

**Post-traumatic findings in eye injuries**

Gonioscopy is crucial after an eye injury to assess potential angle damage, with a comparison between both eyes essential for detecting subtle abnormalities (see the Traumatic Glaucoma chapter). However, gonioscopy should not be performed in suspected or confirmed open globe injuries. Post-traumatic alterations in the angle include:

* **Angle recession:** this involves a laceration between the longitudinal and circular muscles of the ciliary body. Gonioscopic findings include a widened ciliary body band and retroplacement of the iris root in the affected area, compared to other sectors or the same area of the unaffected eye. Hyphema or microhyphema and increased anterior chamber depth may also be indicative of angle recession.
* **Iris disinsertion (or iridodialysis):** this involves rupture of the iris root. Small iris disinsertions can be detected as transillumination defects at the slit lamp.
* **Ciliary body cleft (or cyclodialysis):** this refers to detachment of the ciliary body from the scleral spur. Small clefts may be challenging to detect through gonioscopy alone and may require imaging techniques such as UBM or as OCT and in some cases exploration in the operating theatre.

##### II.1.2.2 Techniques

Gonioscopy should be performed in a dimly-lit room, using a thin slit beam, taking care to avoid shining the light through the pupil. Pupil constriction on light exposure opens the angle, resulting in underestimating the risk of angle closure.

Angle width grading must be performed with the eye in primary position to avoid misclassification. If the patient looks in the direction of the mirror, the angle appears wider and vice versa. A common pitfall is inadvertent pressure over the cornea, which will push back the iris and give an erroneously wide appearance to the angle. All precautions should be taken to sterilize the goniolens. IOP measurements must be performed before gonioscopy. Both eyes should always be examined. (See Fc IV and V ).

###### II.1.2.2.2 Dynamic gonioscopy by indentation or compression

It is recommended to use a small diameter lens for indentation (e.g. 4-mirror). When gentle pressure is applied by the lens on the centre of the cornea, the aqueous humour (AH) and iris are pushed back. In appositional angle closure, the angle can be re-opened. If there is adhesion between the iris and the meshwork, as with goniosynechiae, that portion of angle remains closed ( Fig. II.1.6 \-3).

When pupillary block is the prevalent mechanism, the iris becomes peripherally concave during indentation ( Fig. II.1.6 \-2). In plateau configuration, this iris concavity will not be extended by indentation to the extreme periphery, which is a sign of anteriorly placed ciliary processes called double hump sign ( Fig II.1.5 ). When the crystalline lens has a particularly prominent role in angle closure, indentation causes the iris to move only slightly backwards, retaining a convex profile ( Fig. II.1.6 \-4).

To differentiate appositional from synechial closure “indentation” or “compression” dynamic gonioscopy is essential.

###### II.1.2.2.3 Intraoperative gonioscopy

An essential technique for angle surgery. Proficiency with gonioscopy at the slit lamp is a necessary prerequisite.

Gonioscopy should be performed in every patient being evaluated for glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

Always perform gonioscopy on both eyes of patients with ocular hypertension, suspicion of glaucoma or confirmed glaucoma.

Gonioscopy may affect subsequent IOP measurement and should be performed afterwards.

##### II.1.2.3 Grading of the anterior chamber angle

The use of a grading system for gonioscopy is recommended. It encourages the observer to use a systematic approach in evaluating angle anatomy, allows comparison of findings at different times in the same patients, and classification of the angle.

The Spaeth gonioscopy grading system is the most detailed ( Fig. II.1.7 ).

Other practical grading systems are those of Shaffer and Kanski; both are based on angle width and visibility of the angle structures.

###### II.1.2.3.1 Slit lamp-grading of peripheral AC depth- The Van Herick method

The Van Herick grading ( Fig. II.1.8 ) is an indirect estimation of angle width. The Van Herick technique does not replace gonioscopy but can be a crude case-finding tool to prompt verification by gonioscopy.

This technique is based on the use of corneal thickness as a unit measure of the depth of the anterior chamber at the furthest periphery, preferably on the temporal side. The slit lamp light beam should be at 60 degrees. Grade 0 represents iridocorneal contact, i.e., angle closure. A space between iris and corneal endothelium of less than 1/4 corneal thickness is interpreted as a high risk of anatomical angle closure. When the space is between 1/4 and 1/2 corneal thickness the grade is 2, with a very low risk of angle closure. A grade 3 is not occludable, with an irido/endothelial distance more than 1/2 corneal thickness. Alternatively, the peripheral anterior chamber depth may be expressed as a percentage of the peripheral corneal width.

The Van Herick technique does not replace gonioscopy but can be a crude case-finding tool to prompt verification by gonioscopy

##### II.1.2.4 Anterior segment imaging techniques

Anterior segment imaging such as ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM), anterior segment OCTs (AS-OCT) and Scheimpflug cameras can be useful in some circumstances but cannot replace gonioscopy. Added to gonioscopy, imaging techniques may help elucidate the mechanism of angle closure. UBM can be particularly helpful as – in contrast to AS-OCT – it can image tissues behind the iris (anteriorly placed iris processes in plateau iris, tumours, cysts). Anterior segment imaging provides quantitative angle measurements and helps document the chamber angle dynamics with different light conditions. Anterior segment imaging may classify more eyes as having angle closure than gonioscopy, thus leading to overdiagnosis. Automated 360° goniophotography is also available.

A recent meta-analysis indicated that AS-OCT was not superior to the Van Herick test in detecting angle closure, OCT for angle evaluation has proven to be useful in virtual clinic settings as it allows for asynchronous evaluation of the angle.

Unlike gonioscopy, where various lenses provide similar optical quality, the definition of an AS-OCT scan greatly depends on the specific technology and settings. For example, spectral-domain OCT may not always identify the scleral spur, which is used as a landmark for angle-closure detection, whereas Schwalbe’s line is more easily identified. Some devices allow simultaneous scanning of multiple quadrants, while most only allow scanning one sector at a time. The superior quadrant is not adequately assessed by AS-OCT due to the presence of the lid.

These differences make the results of AS-OCT studies weakly generalizable. Again, diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms are based on gonioscopy and AS-OCT results alone cannot be directly translated into clinical decisions.

Anterior chamber angle imaging devices can be useful to identify the iris configuration of a narrow angle, to assess the influence of the lens, for triage or in iris where the angle cannot be visualised by gonioscopy. However, anterior chamber angle imaging should not replace gonioscopy since features such as peripheral anterior synechia, pigment and other secondary causes of trabecular dysfunction may be missed.

#### II.1.3 Optic nerve head and retinal nerve fibre layer

Glaucoma changes the appearance of the ONH, particularly the neuroretinal rim and vessels, and the RNFL in a characteristic fashion.

Contour changes can best be appreciated with a magnified stereoscopic view preferably through a dilated pupil. Interim examinations, aimed at detecting striking features such as disc haemorrhages, may be performed through an undilated pupil. Stereoscopic examination of the posterior pole is best performed at the slit lamp with either:

* – Indirect non-contact fundus lens with sufficient magnification
* – Direct contact fundus lens

The direct ophthalmoscope is used for monoscopic view of ONH and RNFL examination (Fig. II). The clinical evaluation of the ONH and RNFL should assess the following features.

##### II.1.3.1 Clinical examination

###### II.1.3.1.1 Neuroretinal rim

In a healthy eye, the shape of the rim is influenced by size, shape and tilting of the ONH. The disc is usually slightly vertically oval, often more so in African ancestry subjects who may also have larger discs. In medium-size discs, the neuroretinal rim is typically at least as wide at the 12 and 6 o’clock positions as elsewhere and usually widest in the inferotemporal sector, followed by the supero-temporal, nasal and then temporal sectors ( Fig. II.1.9 ). This pattern, described as ISNT distribution, is less obvious in larger discs, in which the rim is distributed more evenly and in a smaller discs where cupping may not be evident. In small discs the changes associated with glaucoma may not result in cupping, but ‘saucerization’ of the disc surface instead. In large optic discs the normal rim width is relatively narrow and can potentially be misinterpreted as glaucomatous. The exit of the optic nerve from the eye may be oblique, giving rise to a tilted disc. Tilted discs are more common in myopic eyes, and show a wider, gently sloping rim in one disc sector in the direction of the tilt and a narrower, more sharply-defined rim in the opposite sector. Discs in highly myopic eyes are even harder to interpret.

Glaucoma is characterised by progressive narrowing of the neuroretinal rim. The pattern of rim loss varies and may take the form of diffuse narrowing, localised notching, or both in combination. Narrowing of the rim, while occurring in all disc sectors, is generally more common and greatest at the inferior and superior poles (Fig. II.I.10).

###### II.1.3.1.2 Retinal nerve fibre layer

The RNFL appearance can be best assessed in the central 60° at the posterior pole with a blue filter photograph. Clinically at the slit lamp, the RNFL is best evaluated with a red-free light and low magnification and/or with a short, narrow beam of bright white light at high magnification around the circumference of the optic disc within about two-disc diameters of the disc margin. The RNFL surface is best seen if the focus is adjusted just anterior to the main retinal vessels. The fibre bundles are seen as radial silver striations around the disc, slit-like. Groove- like, or spindle-shaped apparent defects, narrower than the retinal vessels, may be seen in the normal fundus. The RNFL may become less visible with age and is more difficult to see in less pigmented fundi. Local (wedge and slit) defects are seen as dark bands, wider than retinal vessels which will extend to the disc margin. These local defects are more easily seen than generalised thinning of the RNFL, which manifests as a loss of brightness and density of striations. When the RNFL is thinned, the blood vessel walls appear sharp against a matt and mottled back- ground. The initial abnormality in glaucoma may be either diffuse thinning or localised defects.

###### II.1.3.1.3 Optic disc haemorrhages

A large proportion of glaucoma patients has optic disc haemorrhages at one time or another ( Fig. II.1.11 ) and sometimes are very subtle. Often overlooked at clinical examinations, they are easier to find in photographs. OCT cannot visualise disc haemorrages. Disc haemorrhages can also be overseen when they persist for periods shorter than the examination schedule. The clinical examination should include actively looking for disc haemorrhages. Many studies have shown that optic disc haemorrhages are associated with a higher risk for glaucomatous VF progression in the next 2 years.

###### II.1.3.1.4 Vessels at the optic disc

Narrowing of the neuroretinal tissue will change the position of the vessels at the optic disc with bending, bayoneting or baring of circumlinear vessels. Those positional changes are particularly important to observe when looking for progression, and can be detected with sequential photographs. It is important to remember that circumlinear vessels can help to detect the inner edge of the rim and are not a sign of glaucoma _per se_ ; the suspicion of disease may arise when the rim recedes and leaves a space under them.

###### II.1.3.1.5 Parapapillary atrophy

Parapapillary atrophy can be differentiated into an alpha zone, which is present in most eyes, and into a beta zone, which is present in some normal eyes and in a high percentage of eyes with glaucoma. Beta parapapillary atrophy is common in myopic and older eyes. In clinical practice, a large beta zone can be regarded as a clue, but not as a definite sign of glaucoma ( Fig. II.1.12 ), However, the area can increase in glaucomatous patients during follow-up.

###### II.1.3.1.6 Optic disc size (vertical disc diameter)

The optic disc size greatly varies in the population. The width of the rim and the size of the cup vary with the overall size of the disc. The mean vertical disc diameter is approximately 1.9 mm. The vertical diameter of the optic disc can be measured at the slit lamp using a hand held high power convex lens. The slit beam should be coaxial with the observation axis; a narrow beam is used to measure the vertical disc diameter using the inner margin of the white Elschnig’s ring as the reference. For quantification, a correction factor needs to be used depending on the magnification of the handheld lens; in clinical practice it is rarely used.

###### II.1.3.1.7 Rim width and cupping

The traditional use of cup/disc ratio (CDR) to classify patients is not recommended and the attention should be focused on the neuroretinal rim such as colour, rim width, intra and inter eye asymmetry and irregularity in distribution ( Fig. II.1.14 ).

###### II.1.3.2.1 Quantitative imaging-Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)

Quantitative imaging of the ONH, retinal nerve fibre layer and inner macular layers using OCT are used widely to assist glaucoma diagnosis and to detect glaucomatous progression during follow-up. Neither fundus photography nor OCT should replace clinical examination and VF testing.

See details about OCT testing and interpretation in the EGS book “Glaucoma Imaging” (2024): _[https://www.eugs.org/educational\_materials/147](https://www.eugs.org/educational_materials/147)_

Embedded Image

OCT is based on short-coherence interferometry and is the most widely used test to document glaucomatous retinal and optic nerve head damage. Current instruments are spectral domain and swept-source OCT systems. Their technical, software and reference database characteristics vary also among manufacturers; therefore, values measured with different OCT devices are not interchangeable. Three main parameter groups are measured and analysed for classification and detection of progression: ONH, peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer and macular inner retinal layers. Interpretation of apparent progression in OCT has to be done with caution due to the possible variability of the measurements, the effect of aging, and possible changes nonrelated to glaucoma. In cases of advanced loss, progression analysis may be beyond the dynamic range of the instrument.

OCT angiography is a rapidly evolving technology for visualizing the retinal and optic nerve

head microvasculature. The role of which is not yet defined in glaucoma management.

###### II.1.3.2.2 OCT for glaucoma diagnosis

OCT imaging instruments typically provide three potential outcomes: ‘within normal limits’, ‘borderline’ and ‘outside normal limits’. This represents a statistical result comparing the individuals’ values with normative database of healthy eyes. OCT is a valuable diagnosis support system but does no replace clinical diagnosis. Therefore, an interpretation of the results in the context of all clinical data is mandatory. Imaging artefacts and software segmentation errors can occur and are more frequent in eyes that are highly myopic or have tilted discs. The clinician should carefully assess the quality of the image and segmentation analysis and judge whether the reference database is relevant for the particular patient.

When assessing for glaucomatous damage, clinicians should integrate data from the optic nerve head (ONH), peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), and macular parameters (see programmes). Evaluation should include both quantitative thickness measurements and qualitative analysis of deviation maps to enhance diagnostic accuracy.

The various imaging technologies have their own advantages and limitations, and their classifications show only partial agreement with clinical exams in diagnosing glaucoma. Diagnosis of glaucoma based on results from one specific exam should be avoided.

Hence, an OCT test “outside normal limits” may be a false positive and does not necessarily indicate that the subject has glaucoma.

###### II.1.3.2.3 Detection of progression with OCT

Most commercial imaging devices have software for quantifying glaucomatous progression, including the rate of progression. These results may serve as additional tools for the assessment of glaucomatous progression but need careful interpretation in conjunction with other tests. As with any other test high quality baseline images are particularly important. The user should assess the test series for the quality of images and software analysis before including the software output in the assessment of the patient.

Several studies have shown that agreement between structural progression and functional deterioration is only partial because of the measurement variability of both structural and functional tests. The structure–function relationship in glaucoma progression depends on disease stage: OCT detects change earlier in mild disease, shows a linear relationship with structural loss in moderate stages, and reaches a floor effect in advanced glaucoma, where functional tests better detect worsening

Most commercially available software for OCT follow-up analysis do not compensate for aging, therefore statistically significant slopes do not necessarily mean true glaucomatous progression. As mentioned above results acquired with different instruments are not interchangeable and cannot be used for longitudinal analysis.

###### II.1.3.2.4 Programmes

To assess retinal ganglion cells, three programs are used in clinically practice. OCT can quantify them in the ONH, around ONH in the peripapillary area and in the macula. Rim width is assessed in the ONH, RNFL in the peripapillary area and ganglion cell complex in the macula.

All parameters can be used to discriminate glaucomatous eyes in mild to moderate stages. OCT has relatively limited value in advanced disease because of a floor effect: under these circumstances it is clinically more useful to examine the GCC rather than the RNFL. Absolute values of the parameters are different from one OCT to another, thus using the same machine or system for follow up is recommended.

#### II.1.4 Perimetry

##### II.1.4.1 Perimetry techniques

Visual field (VF) testing plays a central role in the diagnosis and in the management of glaucoma. Loss of visual function is associated with loss of quality of life, and it is therefore necessary to monitor each glaucoma patient’s VF status.

Static computerised perimetry is preferred in glaucoma management. Kinetic, e.g. Goldmann perimetry, is not suitable for detection of early glaucomatous field loss, since small defects can often be missed between isopters. Computerised perimetry is also less subjective since the results are numerical and tools for computer-assisted interpretation are available. Manual kinetic perimetry may be useful in end-stage disease and in the patients unable to perform automated perimetry.

###### II.1.4.1.1 Automated threshold perimetry

The term Standard Automated Perimetry (SAP) refers to static computerised threshold perimetry performed using standard Goldmann white stimuli on a white background and is the recommended technique in glaucoma management.

Testing algorithms and programs

Various perimeters attempt to estimate perimetric threshold sensitivity using different testing algorithms and patterns. Frequently used threshold algorithms in the Humphrey Visual Field Analyzer (Zeiss Meditec, Dublin, CA, USA), which is the most used perimeter, are Swedish interactive threshold algorithm (SITA) Standard, SITA Fast and SITA Faster. In the Octopus perimeter (Haag-Streit AG, Köniz, Switzerland) the Dynamic Strategy is often recommended for glaucoma diagnosis and follow up. The Octopus TOP algorithm (tendency-oriented perimetry) differs considerably from the SITA and Dynamic strategies. In glaucoma patients and glaucoma suspects, perimetry is usually performed using a Goldmann size III stimulus in the central 24° or 30° field, where the great majority of retinal ganglion cells are located. The VF outside 30° is seldom tested. In recent years it has sometimes been recommended to perform additional testing focusing on the central 10° of the field, in order to detect more central field loss. EGS does not recommend decreasing the frequency of standard 24° or 30° testing by replacing these tests with 10° tests. Such additional testing may be reserved for eyes where structure/function findings do not agree, e.g., in eyes with normal central 24° or 30° VFs but pathological or suspect optic nerve or RNFL findings. Central field loss is very common in glaucoma and such loss at very central points, often referred to as ‘threat to fixation’ is clinically worrisome since central VF defects can be symptomatic and compromise the ability to drive. Macular-enriched grids such as the Humphrey 24-2C have been developed to improve detection of central damage while still covering the peripheral field; although they may offer a useful compromise, current support in the literature remains limited.

As far as possible, it is advantageous to follow patients using a consistent test pattern and strategy, as well as the same technology in order to facilitate detection and quantification of change. In eyes with advanced VF loss, it may be advantageous to switch to a larger stimulus size, e.g. to a Goldmann size V stimulus rather than size III, or to a test point pattern which focuses more closely on the remaining area of functioning vision. In most perimeters one may use test point patterns examining only the central 10° of the field in eyes which have severe loss of paracentral and peripheral function or only ‘tunnel’ fields left.

###### II.1.4.1.2 Non-conventional perimetry

Some modalities of computerised perimetry use testing stimuli that differ from those used in SAP. Examples include SWAP, frequency doubling technology (FDT), and flicker perimetry. These techniques were developed with the hope that they would be able to recognise glaucomatous field loss earlier than conventional SAP but, since such evidence is lacking, they are not recommended for glaucoma management.

###### II.1.4.1.3 Patient instructions

The role of the perimetric technician is of greatest importance in patients who are new to automated perimetric testing. Perimetrically inexperienced patients will produce more reliable test results if the operator simply explains what to expect and how to respond to stimuli. It is, however, very important to point out to perimetric novices, before the first few tests, that many stimuli will be very dim and difficult to see and that even subjects with normal VFs will not see all the stimuli. Without such instructions and explanations many patients will experience perimetry negatively. A demonstration lasting just a few seconds, in which the naïve patient sees what the stimuli look like, where they will appear and how they change brightness will help the patient understand the test, and will reduce patient anxiety, thus making patients more willing to return for future perimetric testing. Most experienced patients require only minimal re-instruction. However, even with experienced patients, the operator should remain in the vicinity of the perimeter in order to hear and respond to any patient queries. A quiet, dimly lit environment is necessary. All personnel performing visual fields should have taken enough threshold perimetry tests themselves to understand first-hand what it is like being tested.

**The learning effect**

Many subjects show an improvement in performance reflected as improved reliability and sensitivity over the first few tests.

##### II.1.4.2 Interpreting test results

Most perimeters provide test results and analyses in paper or electronic reports containing different maps of the VF plus summary indices and other interpretations.

###### II.1.4.2.1 Test data elements commonly seen in perimetry reports

* The numerical threshold map provides the ‘raw’ estimated threshold values at each test point location.
* The grey scale maps provide a graphical representation of the numerical threshold map, while in the Octopus perimeter the colour-coded maps provide a graphical representation of the deviations from age-corrected normal values.
* The numerical total deviation map shows point-wise differences between the age- corrected normal threshold sensitivity at each test point location and the patient’s measured threshold value.
* The numerical pattern deviation map and the corrected deviation map show the same values but after correction for any diffuse loss of sensitivity. Thus, both types of deviation maps highlight localised field loss.
* Probability maps are very important, since they provide the statistical significance of the numerical deviations, compared to age corrected normative data.

###### II.1.4.2.2 Reliability indices

These indices are meant to estimate the reliability of test results and were developed in the early days of automated perimetry. Over time it has become clear that these indices are themselves not very reliable. Thus, high frequencies of false negative (FN) responses have been shown to be of relatively little value in the evaluation of glaucomatous VFs, since abnormal fields often have high FN values even in patients who are very attentive and responsive. The impact of FNs varies with disease severity. While FNs hold little value in patients with moderate to severe disease, they may provide useful information in cases of suspected glaucoma or early-stage disease. High rates of fixation losses (FL) assessed using the blind spot technique may indicate poor fixation, but if the blind spot position is erroneously located, a high FL rate will be indicated even if fixation is perfect. It is probably better to rely on the automatic eye/ gaze tracker of the perimeter or on the judgement of the perimetrist. FLs have limited effect on test-retest variability, so a test with high FLs should not always be considered as unreliable. High frequencies of false positive (FP) answers, may be a sign of poor reliability, but many tests with relatively high FP rates have been found to provide useful information. Most patients will deliver very useful perimetry test results if properly instructed, and exams should not be discarded only because one or more reliability parameters has been flagged by the instrument’s software.

###### II.1.4.2.3 Visual field indices

VF indices are numbers summarising perimetric test results. MD (mean deviation in the Humphrey or mean defect in the Octopus) is indicative of the average difference between age-corrected normal sensitivity and measured threshold sensitivity values at all test point locations. The visual field index (VFI - Humphrey) is similar to the MD but more heavily centre-weighted. VFI results are expressed in percent rather than in decibels and are more resistant to cataract effects, compared to MD. The Humphrey

PSD and the Octopus loss variance (LV) index are designed to detect localised loss. In general, global indices are not primarily meant for and should not be used alone for diagnosis.

###### II.1.4.2.4 Interpretation methods and aids

A first-time normal exam can be accepted if reliable, but a first-time apparently abnormal exam should be repeated and confirmed if not consistent with other clinical findings i.e., with the appearance of the optic nerve and RNFL.

Analysis of single field test results, based on clustered points

Clusters of test point locations with significantly reduced sensitivity are more reliable indicators of early glaucomatous field loss than are an equal number of significantly depressed points that are randomly scattered about the VF. One rule which is often used to classify a test result as outside normal limits requires a minimum of three clustered points having significantly depressed sensitivity, among which at least one should have a significance of p<1%.

The Bebié curve

The Bebié curve, which is also known as the cumulative defect curve of the Octopus perimeter, is a summary graph of localised and diffuse sensitivity loss. In entirely diffuse loss the overall curve shows reduced sensitivity compared to normal. This is typically associated with media opacities and not with glaucoma. In focal loss, the right part of the curve is depressed as compared to the normal reference curve. Focal loss is much more consistent with a diagnosis of glaucoma than is diffuse loss.

The Glaucoma Hemifield Test (GHT)

The Glaucoma Hemifield Test of the Humphrey perimeter was developed specifically to examine clusters of points relevant to glaucoma. It classifies results as ‘within normal limits’, ’outside normal limits’ or ‘borderline’. Other GHT classifications are ‘general depression of sensitivity’, typically found in eyes with media opacities but no manifest glaucoma, and ‘abnormally high sensitivity’ which indicates that the patient has pressed the response button even when non-perceptible stimuli were presented. Importantly, the GHT primarily detects abnormalities based on asymmetry between the superior and inferior hemifields; as such, symmetric arcuate defects which are not uncommon in glaucoma may still produce a result ‘within normal limits’.

###### II.1.4.2.5 Confirmation of classification

Field defects which appear clearly glaucomatous, and which are consistent with other clinical findings usually do not need confirmation to support a diagnosis. VFs with subtle defects may require confirmatory tests (See Fc VI ).

###### II.1.4.2.6 Detecting and quantifying glaucomatous visual field deterioration

It is important to detect and also to quantify VF deterioration in patients under care for glaucoma (see Fc VII ). Be aware that progression software may automatically exclude tests flagged as unreliable, even though such tests can still provide clinically valuable information. There are two main approaches to computer-assisted VF progression analyses:

* Event analyses
* Progression event analyses seek to detect whether or not a statistically significant VF change has occurred. Indices or test points/clusters are flagged if they have deteriorated more than the expected test-retest variation. Event based analyses have been used in large randomised controlled glaucoma trials, e.g. EMGT, AGIS, CIGTS and UKGTS (See Ch I.1.7 ). In clinical practice, event analysis is complementary to trend analyses, especially for detecting focal damage. Event analyses usually require confirmation testing.

* Trend analyses
* Regression analysis to determine the VF rate of progression is widely accepted and is strongly recommended in the management of eyes having glaucomatous field loss. The perimetric rate of progression is the velocity of worsening of the VF and is usually quantified by using linear regression analysis over time of the global indices MD or VFI. Rate of progression is expressed in dB/year or in %/year. Plotting the MD or VFI value of an eye over time can show if the observed rate of progression is likely to lead to loss of QoL during the patient’s expected life-time. PSD and LV should not be used for trend analysis, because in early disease they increase as the field worsens but then peak and start decreasing again as VF damage becomes moderate to advanced. Trend based analysis in the form of pointwise linear regression has been used in large scale studies such as the LoGTS RCT and a landmark cohort study relating optic disc haemorrhage to VF progression (See Ch I.1.7 ).

* Number and frequency of tests
* Determining the rate of progression of an individual eye usually requires a significant time span, typically at least two years, and enough field tests. It has been proposed that newly diagnosed glaucoma patients should be tested with SAP three times per year during the first two years after diagnosis. In this way rate of progression can be determined early, and rapidly progressing eyes can be revealed with great certainty. Most often, the frequency of testing can then be reduced and tailored to the observed progression rate, and to the stage of disease. Patients with OHT do not need frequent VF testing; once every one or two years is often sufficient.

##### II.1.4.2.7 Other perimeters

It should be noted that, although this Chapter has focused on two perimeter brands, the Octopus and the Humphrey, alternative devices by several different manufacturers are available and more are under development.

Several promising technologies for home-based perimetry have been identified. However, current studies have primarily been conducted in controlled settings with highly selective populations. The effectiveness and value of home-based perimetry for glaucoma remain uncertain. Further research is needed to determine its capability in detecting glaucoma and monitoring disease progression under real-world conditions.

#### II.1.5 Artificial intelligence

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionising healthcare. AI applications in glaucoma use clinical data, fundus photography, OCT, and VF data to diagnose the disease, monitor its progression, and predict future developments. Studies have shown a high accuracy of AI algorithms in diagnosing glaucoma and detecting its progression. Additionally, AI tools may be useful for patient risk profiling. However, several challenges must be addressed before widespread clinical adoption.

##### II.1.5.1 Key challenges

* – **Model Generalisability:** AI models may lack the ability to generalise across different populations and clinical settings due to limited and non-representative training data.
* – **Data Quality:** AI performance heavily depends on data quality.
* – **Data Quantity:** AI models, particularly deep learning (DL), require vast amounts of data. In glaucoma, large-scale, standardised datasets are scarce, limiting model robustness.
* – **Difficulties assessing ground truth:** establishing a reliable ground truth, as clinical diagnosis often involves subjective interpretation of imaging and functional tests, leading to variability even among expert clinicians.
* – **Model Interpretability (Black-Box Issue):** Many AI models operate as black boxes, making it difficult for clinicians to understand their decision-making processes, reducing trust.
* – **Data Ownership and Privacy:** Data-sharing across institutions raises concerns over ownership and privacy, complicating efforts to create large, centralised datasets.
* – **Poor uncertainty estimations.**
* – **Cost and Accessibility:** AI tools are not yet available for everyday clinical settings and future costs are uncertain.

##### II.1.5.2 Solutions and future directions

* – **Federated Learning:** Federated learning enables external access for the training of AI models on data that does not leave the health institution. Model updates are combined centrally, maintaining data privacy while creating robust AI models across multiple institutions. This solves concerns about data ownership and privacy.
* – **Generative AI for Data Scarcity:** Generative AI models like Generative Adversarial Networks can generate synthetic medical images, which are virtually indistinguishable from real ones and help address data scarcity while preserving patient privacy.
* – **Improving Interpretability:** New techniques like saliency/heat maps, attention mechanisms, and Vision Transformers help make AI models more transparent, allowing clinicians to see how models generate their predictions.
* – **International Collaboration:** Pooling data through international collaborations can enhance data diversity and quantity, improving model generalisability and robustness.
* – **Multimodal Models:** Combining data from various sources (OCT, VFs, fundus photography) can create more accurate models that offer comprehensive insights into glaucoma diagnosis and progression.
* – **Regulations for Data Security:** New regulations are needed to protect not only personal data but also the integrity of AI models, ensuring secure and ethical deployment in clinical practice.
* – **Screening cost-effectiveness:** AI-based diagnostic screening tools and risk profiling may allow screening to become more cost-effective.

**AI is transforming glaucoma care** : High accuracy in diagnosis, progression monitoring, and risk profiling.

At present, there is **not enough evidence to support AI algorithms in clinical practice.**

**Key Challenges** : Generalisability, data quality & quantity, black-box models, privacy concerns, and accessibility.

**Future Solutions** : Federated learning, generative AI, multimodal models, improved interpretability, global collaboration, and data security regulations.

#### II.1.6 Genetics

Many forms of congenital and juvenile glaucoma are linked to specific genetic mutations, but management of these conditions is based on the phenotype, i.e. the clinical presentation. The remainder of this section deals with genetic influences on POAG, since this is responsible for the greatest burden of disease of the glaucomas. The search for the genetic basis of POAG was prompted by epidemiological findings, for example that first degree relatives of glaucoma patients are at considerably higher risk of developing the condition. The areas of the genome associated with POAG can be divided into Mendelian mutations and complex variants.

##### II.1.6.1 Mendelian mutations

Mendelian diseases are usually caused by single genetic defects which are rare and strongly linked to the development of disease. Environmental factors and variants elsewhere in the genome apart from the causative mutation do not affect the presence or absence of disease. The most common Mendelian forms of POAG are caused by mutations in the myocilin (MYOC) gene. The prevalence of MYOC mutations has been estimated as 2-4% in POAG patients, but if patients are preferentially selected based on young age of onset, high IOP and strong family history the prevalence rises to 16-40%. As an example, a young, currently unaffected member of a family which carries a MYOC mutation may benefit from genetic testing to discover whether she/he has the mutation. If negative for MYOC this subject has no excess risk for POAG; if posititve close monitoring and early treatment may be useful to prevent future vision loss. However, the advisability of genetic testing will depend on a number of factors such as details about the condition and its prognosis, the inheritance pattern, and the risk to children or other family members. Counselling for at-risk but currently unaffected family members should explore the underlying motivation for genetic testing and explain the testing process and the potential impact of the test result.

##### II.1.6.2 Complex variants

In contrast to Mendelian mutations, variants which contribute to complex disease occur in numerous genes, are more common and have a relatively small effect size. The conceptual framework posits that multiple genetic variants, in conjunction with environmental factors, interact to contribute to disease development. With the advent of genome-wide association studies hundreds of such variants associated with POAG, IOP and disc morphology have been discovered. Variants associated with IOP have been incorporated into a genetic prediction model for POAG and a variant in the TMCO1 gene has been incorporated into the risk calculator for conversion from ocular hypertension to POAG in the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS). Though the contribution of complex variants to the diagnosis and management of POAG is constantly and rapidly improving it is currently not appropriate to use these variants as a basis for genetic screening.

**Do not offer genotyping routinely to adult glaucoma patients.**

##### II.1.6.3 Third party genotyping

Individuals may present to healthcare services seeking advice about the results of their genotypes which have been obtained from direct-to-consumer private companies or as a result of volunteering for research studies. Such genetic information is usually not subject to the same quality control measures as in clinical genetics services so the results may be misleading. For example, the false positive rate for some BRCA gene variants in the UK Biobank was more than 84%. Thus, third party genotyping measures should not currently be used for clinical decision making.

Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) estimate the combined effect of many genetic variants on an individual’s relative risk of disease. They have also been used in glaucoma to predict progression and response to treatment. This approach holds hope for the future but currently no PRS has been validated for clinical use.

**Genetic information obtained by third party commercial services should be considered with regard to the accuracy and reliability of the providing service, and any decison making resulting from it must be integrated into the clinical context of the specific patient.**

### II.2 Classification and terminology

#### II.2.1 Childhood glaucoma

Childhood glaucoma is a group of challenging diseases because of its rare occurrence, heterogeneous phenotype and its various underlying conditions. Examination can be difficult due to low cooperation. An immediate therapy performed by a well-coordinated interdisciplinary team of an experienced glaucoma surgeon, paediatric ophthalmologists, pediatricians and anaesthetists is necessary to prevent blindness. Nevertheless, most children will suffer a significant impairment of vision and quality of life. Surgical treatment is necessary in nearly all cases. See below and Ch II.3.14.2 .

#### II.2.1.1 Classification

Childhood glaucoma is classified into primary and secondary types following the Childhood Glaucoma Research Network ( [CGRN-ChildhoodGlaucoma.com](https://cgrn-childhoodglaucoma.com/) ) (see table II.3 ).

Caveat: The current age-based classification does not take into account the genetic background. This classification rather reflects the prognosis than the pathophysiology.

#### II.2.1.2 Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG)

Epidemiology :

Congenital glaucoma occurs in about 1 in 12-18,000 births among white Europeans. Incidence can be 5 to 10 times higher if consanguinity of parents is present. Severe visual disability is common. PCG is more common in males (65%), and is bilateral in 70% of patients. Isolated angle dysgenesis or dysgenesis involving the trabecular meshwork (trabeculodysgenesis) is the most common form of primary congenital glaucoma.

Aetiology/mechanism :

Angle dysgenesis is caused by incomplete development of the TM/outflow system before and/or after birth. There is a primarily monogenic influence, however, polygenic patterns are a current subject of research. Heredity shows recessive inheritance with variable penetrance in most cases or is sporadic. The most common associated gene is CYP1B1, others are TEK/ANGPT1, LTBP2, MYOC and EFEMP1. Genetic testing is recommended to rule out other congenital abnormalities, to facilitate consultation in regard of family planning of both patients and parents and to help coping and disease management. Consanguinity increases the risk of the disease severity and is considered as a poor prognostic factor.

Decreased aqueous outflow due to trabeculodysgenesis causes significant elevation of IOP. High IOP may lead to buphthalmos and to optic neuropathy.

Symptoms and findings (see Table II.4 ) :

* – Not always symptomatic
* – Photophobia, tearing, blepharospasm, and eye rubbing are typical early signs
* – Crying, unhappy child during first weeks or year of life may raise suspicion
* – Large eyes/buphthalmos with large corneal diameters and Haab striae
* – Disc cupping typically occurs only after some months and may reverse following successful treatment
* – Gonioscopic signs: anterior insertion of the iris, forming a scalloped line with persistent uveal tissue and poorly differentiated structures as a sign of trabeculodysgenesis

Certain diagnostic criteria likely carry more weight than others e.g. Haab striae, axial length. The diagnostic value of IOP alone is insufficient to make a diagnosis of PCG because IOP in children underlies substantial fluctuations depending on the setting and on the child. Threshold for normal IOP is not comparable to adults. Usually, the best values are taken in the cooperative, calm and awake child using hand-held tonometers, however, the choice of measurement method is at the discretion of the investigator. A measurement taken in a crying awake child can cause falsely high values, on the other hand, most anaesthetics cause falsely low values. Besides applanation tonometry, rebound tonometry is a valid option in childhood glaucoma and can also be used for home tonometry. Haab striae are a strong indicator for congenital glaucoma. Corneal diameter should be monitored over time. If it exceeds the age-related normal growth it can be a sign of uncontrolled IOP. Central corneal thickness should also be measured as it can be increased also without corneal oedema and possibly influences the IOP values. Epithelial corneal oedema, while leading to underestimation of IOP, is a sign of increased IOP. Corneal pathologies that lead to increased corneal rigidity may overestimate IOP. Digital IOP evaluation (palpation) may be an alternative to estimate IOP.

Axial length is an important value for establishing the diagnosis. It is important for monitoring, as it can give information about the IOP during a given time interval.
