Differential diagnoses :

* – Conjunctivitis
* – Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
* – Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPMD)
* – Corneal hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED)
* – X-linked megalocornea
* – Birth trauma
* – Ocular hypertension
* – Large optic discs

Don’t make decisions based on IOP alone, but look for structural changes of the cornea such as Haab striae, epithelial oedema, corneal enlargement.

Measuring of axial length is crucial for detecting and monitoring of the disease. Consider the high risk of secondary glaucoma in early congenital cataract surgery.

Treatment :

Management of these cases is particularly challenging.

Initial surgery is indicated in nearly all cases with primary congenital glaucoma. Medical treatment is usually neither effective nor practicable in long term. Medications, including oral CAIs can be used while decision is made on a surgical approach and in case of failed surgery while preparing for further options.

Primary surgery: Angle surgery such as early ab interno or ab externo, in case of unclear cornea, trabeculotomy or goniotomy are the recommended first choice procedures. Subsequent filtration surgery or glaucoma drainage devices may be indicated if these are unsuccessful. Combined trabeculotomy/trabeculectomy may be considered in some cases. Cycloablative procedures can be used as interim solution to postpone revision surgery. Other surgeries are usually not recommended for childhood glaucoma.

Life-long follow-up of IOP is mandatory to avoid undetected progression. Orthoptic follow-ups as well as refractive correction are necessary to favor age-appropriate visual development, as **anisometropic amblyopia remains a significant cause of visual morbidity even after adequate intraocular pressure (IOP) control.**

In children, medical treatment can cause several side effects and needs to be applied with caution:

* – Alpha-2-agonists: absolute contraindication age <2 years, relative contraindication age <7 years/body weight <20 kg as well as impaired blood-brain barrier (e.g., in children with Sturge Weber-syndrome and leptomeningeal angiomatosis). Narcolepsy is a side effect in any low body weight individual.
* – Beta blockers: contraindicated especially in preterm and neonates. Possible bradycardia, respiratory depression, monitoring is to be considered, as well as starting with low concentration (0.1% or 0.25%).
* – Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (local/systemic): metabolic acidosis leading to failure to thrive, lethargy, lack of appetite, diarrhoea; not approved for preterm infants born before 36th week and newborns younger than 1 week; oral acetazolamide dose 10 to 15 mg/kg body weight per day, split in 2 to 3 doses (max. daily dose 20mg/kg body weight per day), can be given orally also dissolved in milk (e.g. 50mg/ml).
* – Miotics: pylorospasm with consecutive vomiting possible, not advised in children aged <1 month.
* – Prostaglandins: Travoprost is approved from the age of 2 months; Latanoprost not approved for preterm infants born befoore 36th week.

Systematic review:

* – Gagrani M, Garg I, Ghate D. Surgical interventions for primary congenital glaucoma. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2020, Issue 8. Art. No.: CD008213. DOI: 10.1002/14651858. CD008213.pub3.

#### II.2.1.3 Juvenile Open Angle Glaucoma (JOAG)

Aetiology/mechanism : Estimated prevalence: 1:50.000. Typically manifests between the age of 4 and 35 years. Often includes a variable dysgenesis resembling that of primary congenital glaucoma. Commonly associated with myopia. Inheritance patterns are heterogeneous, with MYOC and CYP1B being the most frequent genetic alterations.

Differentiation from PCG :

* – No ocular or corneal enlargement
* – No congenital ocular anomalies or syndromes
* – May be asymptomatic until visual field loss advanced
* – Frequently asymmetric findings

Features :

* – Open angle
* – Elevated IOP
* – Might exhibit high iris insertion or iris processes on gonioscopy
* – Optic nerve and VF damage depending on disease stage

Treatment :

Medical treatment is more successful than in PCG, however, surgery is frequently necessary (40-70%). Angle surgery (trabeculotomy, goniotomy) or combined angle and filtration surgery can yield good results. Filtering surgeries carry risk of hypotony which is higher in younger patients. Glaucoma drainage implants are an opportunity in refractory cases.

The treatment of **childhood glaucoma** is particularly challenging due to the complex nature of the disease and to the intrinsic difficulties in examining patients at this age and operating on them. Treatment has to be adapted to the primary anomaly, and the mechanism of IOP elevation. Medications may be initiated as a temporary measure especially in PCG. It is recommended that these children should be referred to tertiary care centres with specific expertise. See I.5.4

#### II.2.1.4 Secondary Childhood Glaucoma

A variety of pathogenetic mechanisms are possible. A complete list and extensive discussion are outside the scope of the Guidelines.

Genetic testing is strongly recommended due to the large overlap of phenotypes.

Treatment of secondary childhood glaucoma See Treatment for PCG (II.2.1.2). Secondary childhood glaucoma can be caused by both open angle and angle closure mechanisms. Management to be adapted to the primary anomaly, the mechanism of IOP elevation and the QoL of the patient. These patients require highly specialised care.

##### II.2.1.4.1 Glaucoma associated with non-acquired ocular anomalies

* – Axenfeld Rieger anomaly (Syndrome if systemic associations)
* – Peters anomaly (Peters Plus Syndrome if systemic associations)
* – Aniridia
* – Ectropion uveae
* – Persistent foetal vasculature (if glaucoma present before cataract surgery)
* – Oculodermal melanocytosis (Naevus of Ota)
* – Posterior polymorphous dystrophy
* – Microphthalmos
* – Microcornea
* – Ectopia lentis
* – Nanophthalmos

Heredity : Heterogeneous phenotypes with fluent transitions between anterior segment syndromes are possible. Genetic testing may help to differentiate between the syndromes. However, also the genotype can be variable.

Axenfeld Rieger Anomaly (ARA) usually has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, with a high association with FOXC1 and PITX2 alterations. ARA causes glaucoma in 50 to 75%, thus relatives should be screened for elevated IOP and glaucoma.

Aniridia is associated with mutations in PAX6 (autosomal dominant pattern). WT1 is an adjacent gene to PAX6 and can be altered as well, causing a higher risk for nephroblastoma (WAGR syndrome: Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, retardation). Thus, WT1 should be assessed as well.

##### II.2.1.4.2 Glaucoma associated with non-acquired systemic disease or syndrome

* – Chromosomal disorders such as Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
* – Connective tissue disorders: Marfan syndrome Weill-Marchesani syndrome, Stickler syndrome
* – Metabolic disorders: Homocysteinuria, Lowe syndrome, Mucopolysaccharidoses
* – Neurocutaneous syndromes (Phacomatoses): Neurofibromatosis 1 and 2, Sturge-Weber Syndrome, Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber Syndrome, Rubinstein-Taybi
* – Congenital rubella

Association with systemic disease or syndrome usually requires interdisciplinary approach Close cooperation with pediatricians, paediatric ophthalmologists and orthoptists is mandatory.

##### II.2.1.4.3 Glaucoma associated with acquired ocular conditions

* – Uveitis
* – Trauma (hyphaema, angle recession, ectopia lentis)
* – Steroid induced
* – Tumours (benign/malignant, ocular/orbital)
* – Retinopathy of prematurity

##### II.2.1.4.4 Glaucoma following childhood cataract surgery (GFCS)

Secondary glaucoma is a frequent serious complication after cataract surgery in early infancy. The incidence may increase up to 50% if cataract surgery is performed before the 9th month of life. The younger the child is at time of cataract surgery, the higher the risk of developing secondary glaucoma. Mechanism can be open angle (more often) or angle closure generally due to pupillary block. Low age at cataract surgery and microcornea are the main risk factors for the development of GFCS. The risk for GFCS increases with the time passed after cataract surgery, thus, life-long IOP follow-up is mandatory. Pseudophakia is not a protective factor.

The risk-benefit ratio between amblyopia and glaucoma should be evaluated carefully especially in children with unilateral cataract.

Secondary glaucoma is difficult to treat and often needs glaucoma drainage device surgery for long-term IOP control. However, surgical risks are high in this group of patients and teamwork is instrumental for the treatment of amblyopia in these children.

Treatment has to be adapted to the underlying condition. Medications can be first choice treatment in children with some forms of secondary glaucomas and acquired conditions. IOPs should be checked in every child after cataract surgery and if glaucoma is detected, angle closure should be ruled out. Whenever possible such cases should be referred to tertiary care centres since eyes with associated anomalies/problems might be even more complex.

For patients with systemic disorders a multidisciplinary approach is required.

Systematic review:

* – Jin S, Zhang J, Wang J, et al. Advisability of primary intraocular lens implantation for infants under 2: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Clin Pract 2021;75:e14143.

#### II.2.2 Open Angle Glaucoma

##### II.2.2.1 Primary open angle glaucoma (POAG)

Definition : POAG is a chronic, progressive, potentially blinding, irreversible eye disease causing optic nerve rim and RNFL loss with related VF defects. Angle appearance is normal, and major risk factors include the level of IOP and older age. Visual disability is usually prevented by early diagnosis and treatment.

Aetiology/mechanism :

The aetiology remains unclear. Multiple genetic factors and the influence of co-morbidities are likely to play a role. The current concept of how damage is elicited includes deformation of the lamina cribrosa caused by IOP levels that are not tolerated by the individual eye. This is thought to result in axonal damage with consequent apoptotic death of the retinal ganglion cells. Vascular factors, oxidative stress, inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction also probably play a role.

Any increase in IOP is caused by elevated outflow resistance mainly in the TM outflow pathways. A substantial proportion of patients develop POAG at IOPs within the normal range.

POAG has been arbitrarily subdivided into ’high pressure’ and ’normal-pressure’ disease, even though they represent a spectrum of optic neuropathies. It is presumed that risk factors other than IOP have a relatively greater importance if there is glaucoma at the lower pressure levels. The treatment principles are the same, but there may be some differences in clinical features. Glaucoma with lower IOP levels may be more common in women with vascular dysregulation (e.g. migraine, Raynaud). Disc haemorrhages and paracentral scotomas may be more common (See Fig II.1.11 ).

Epidemiology :

Glaucoma is one of the leading causes of irreversible blindness both in Europe and worldwide. POAG is unusual under the age of 40 years. Its prevalence increases with age.

Risk factors for the onset of POAG :

* – Older age
* – Higher IOP
* – Ethnicity: the prevalence of glaucoma is highest in people of black ancestry (see glaucoma epidemiology, I.6)
* – Low CCT
* – Family history of glaucoma: the risk of having OAG is higher for individuals with a first-degree relative with confirmed OAG
* – Myopia (significant risk increase in high degree myopia)
* – Blood pressure dysregulation
* – Others: cardiovascular diseases, sleep apnoea

Data from the literature on diabetes, systemic high blood pressure, migraine, Raynaud syndrome, Alzheimer´s disease and H. pylori infections are inconsistent.

Risk factors for progression of POAG

Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT), Advanced Glaucoma Intervention Study (AGIS), Collaborative Initial Glaucoma Treatment Study (CIGTS), Collaborative Normal Tension Glaucoma Study (CNTGS) have identified the following risk factors for progression (for details on studies see I.7):

* – Older age
* – Higher IOP
* – Presence of disc haemorrhages
* – Thinner CCT is not independent prognostic factor for progression of OAG in univariate analyses

Treatment :

Choice of primary therapeutic modality needs to be made on an individual patient basis.

###### II.2.2.1.1 Primary late-onset juvenile glaucoma

Aetiology/mechanism : Decreased aqueous outﬂow

Features :

* – Onset: beyond infancy, usually after puberty or early adulthood. Heredity: if familiar frequently dominant trait. Genes associated with primary juvenile glaucoma have been identified as MYOC (see genetics chapter II.1.6)
* – Elevated IOP without treatment
* – ONH and RNFL: Diffuse damage typical, but any type of glaucomatous damage
* – Visual field: glaucomatous defects
* – Gonioscopy: wide open anterior chamber angle, often poorly differentiated
* – No congenital or developmental anomalies

Treatment :

Medical therapy: any effective and well tolerated topical regimen

Surgery: early surgery often required (filtering procedure or goniotomy/ trabeculotomy; consider antimetabolites)

Laser trabeculoplasty: not recommended

###### II.2.2.1.2 Primary open angle glaucoma suspect

Definition : A glaucoma suspect is an individual with clinical findings suggestive but not confirmatory of OAG. There may be a varying combination of borderline results concerning structural and/or functional tests. Often only time will determine whether a glaucoma suspect has early stages of glaucoma or not (See Fc IX).

Features :

* – Visual field and/or optic disc and/or nerve fibre layer normal or suspicious, with at least one being suspicious
* – IOP can be normal or increased

Treatment (See Fc VI):

Risks and benefits of treatment need to be weighed against the risk of the development of glaucomatous damage. The indication for any form of therapy is relative and may be discussed with the patient. In general, treatment is not necessary if the IOP is not elevated. Follow-up at intervals of 6-12 months initially, to be prolonged or the patient discharged if all parameters remain unchanged.

###### II.2.2.1.3 Ocular Hypertension

Features :

* – IOP >21 mmHg without treatment
* – Visual field: normal
* – Optic disc and retinal nerve fiber layer: normal
* – Gonioscopy: open anterior chamber angle (exclude intermittent angle closure, (see II.2.4.1)
* – No history or signs of other eye disease or steroid use

Risk factors for the conversion of OHT to POAG :

The following risk factors and predictive factors were consistently reported in both the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study OHTS and the European Glaucoma Prevention Study EGPS (for details on the studies see I.1.7 ):

* – Older age
* – Higher IOP
* – Thinner CCT

A risk calculator is freely available to estimate the risk of developing glaucoma at 5 years, <https://ohts.wustl.edu/risk/>

Treatment :

Treatment may be advisable in people with high risk of conversion to glaucoma. Other factors like life expectancy, overall health, and the likelihood of meaningful visual impairment also should be taken into account when making de decision to treat.

Increased IOP should be confirmed before starting treatment unless very high. In general offer treatment in patients with repeated IOPs in the high twenties, even without additional risk factors. Treatment principles and choices will be similar to those for POAG. The initial approach is to offer either medical treatment or laser trabeculoplasty.

Follow-up at intervals of 6-12 months initially, to be prolonged if all parameters remain stable. See Fc IX.

Assess each patient individually when deciding whether or not to offer treatment. Involve the patient.

Ask their opinion.

#### II.2.3 Secondary open angle glaucoma

Definition : Secondary open angle glaucomas (OAG) are a heterogeneous group of conditions, in which elevated IOP is the leading pathological factor causing the glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Most forms of secondary glaucoma have complex mechanisms which can overlap or evolve to angle closure.

##### II.2.3.1 Secondary open angle glaucoma caused by ocular disease

###### II.2.3.1.1 Pseudoexfoliative or exfoliative glaucoma (PXFG)

Epidemiology : Pseudoexfoliative glaucoma (PXFG) is the most common type of secondary OAG, its prevalence varies considerably across populations. According to population based data, PXFG develops in approximately 15% to 26% of eyes with OHT and pseudoexfoliation syndrome (PXF) over a 5 year period. PXF/PXFG may be associated with systemic diseases (e.g. vascular diseases, inguinal hernia and female’s pelvic organ prolapse. Progression of PXFG is approximately 3 times faster than that of POAG.

Aetiology/mechanism :

PXFG develops from PXF, in which an abnormal fibrillo-granular protein (pseudoexfoliation material) is produced in the eye.

Genetics : Development of PXF is strongly associated with certain gene variants including LOXL1. The development of PXFG from PXF is probably influenced by environmental factors.

Features :

* – Onset: usually older than 50 years with large between-population variability
* – Pseudoexfoliation material accumulates in a characteristic pattern on the anterior lens capsule - better visualised after pupil dilatation, pupillary margin, TM and the zonules
* – Pigment loss from the pupil margin is common (“moth eaten pupil”)
* – On cross sectional assessment one or both eyes may show clinically signs of PXFG; often bilateral and asymmetrical
* – IOP is higher than that in POAG, and diurnal IOP fluctuation is high
* – VF/ONH damage is frequently advanced in the worse eye at diagnosis
* – The angle can be wide open, narrow or closed when the lens moves anteriorly due to zonular laxity
* – On gonioscopy, Sampaolesi’s line (pigment deposition anterior to Schwalbe’s line) is common and characteristic for PXFG and TM usually shows dense pigmentation, often with uneven distribution (“salt and pepper” appearance)

* – Due to progressive zonular damage, phacodonesis and lens subluxation are not uncommon, and the complication rate of cataract surgery may be increased.
* – Late in-the-bag intraocular lens (IOL) dislocation several years after uncomplicated cataract surgery is not uncommon.

Treatment :

Treatment options for PXFG are similar to those of POAG although there is higher risk of progression in PXFG. Laser trabeculoplasty and medical treatment are equally effective but both lose efficacy over time. In clinically unilateral PXFG the fellow eye also needs to be regularly checked for IOP elevation and glaucoma since the conversion rate is high (see II.3).

###### II.2.3.1.2 Pigmentary glaucoma (PG)

Epidemiology : PG represents 1-1.5% of all glaucoma cases. It is more common in white Caucasian myopic men. It is typically diagnosed at the age of 30-50 years. The reported risk of developing glaucoma in patients with pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS) in clinic populations ranges from 10 to 50%, but this may represent a biased population of individuals with PDS and raised IOP.

Mechanism :

Melanin pigment is released from the iris pigmented epithelium as the result of rubbing between lens zonules and posterior surface of the iris. Posterior bowing of the iris with “reverse pupillary block” configuration is noted in many eyes with pigment dispersion.

Melanin granules cause an increase of TM outflow resistance and hence an elevation of IOP. The current understanding is that TM cells phagocytose pigment, which subsequently leads to their death.

Two entities can be described:

* – PDS: usually bilateral characterized by dispersion of iris pigment, may be associated with elevated IOP
* – PG: glaucomatous optic neuropathy and PDS

Features :

* – Midperipheral iris transillumination with a radial spoke like pattern due to pigment loss best visible with retroillumination
* – Pigment deposition in the corneal endothelium typically accumulating vertically as Krukenberg spindle (frequently seen, but not pathognomonic)
* – Homogenously dark brown, densely pigmented TM
* – Pigment deposition along the insertion of the zonular fibres into the lens, known as Scheie stripe’ or ‘Zentmayer’s ring’
* – Very deep anterior chamber with backward bowing of the peripheral iris (see gonioscopy chapter)
* – Transient blurry vision due to IOP spikes (often after exercise or pupillary dilatation)

Treatment :

Treatment of PG is similar to that of POAG. No PG-specific treatment is available. Laser trabeculoplasty and medical treatment are equally effective, but spikes of IOP are common after laser trabeculoplasty and so should be performed cautiously with low power settings and with prophylactic treatment to prevent IOP spikes (see II.3). Peripheral iridotomy is controversial but may be considered in selected patients.

###### II.2.3.1.3 Lens-induced open angle glaucoma

Aetiology/mechanism :

In lens-induced OAG, TM outflow pathways are obstructed by lens particles and/or inflammatory cells.

* – Phacoemulsificationlytic glaucoma: the TM is obstructed by lens material leaking from mature or hypermature cataract
* – Traumatic lens injury: the TM is obstructed by lens particles from a traumatically or surgically injured lens
* – Phacoemulsificationanaphylactic glaucoma: lens proteins lead to granulomatous uveitis affecting the TM

Features :

* – Unilateral pain with redness and inflammation
* – Reduced vision and elevated IOP
* – Signs of injured lens and/or mature/hypermature cataract are present, with or with- out anterior uveitis (aqueous flare and keratic precipitates)

Treatment :

Intensive topical steroids and IOP lowering medications, extraction of lens or lens fragments, vitrectomy if needed.

###### II.2.3.1.4 Glaucoma associated with intraocular haemorrhage

Aetiology/mechanism :

Non-traumatic acute bleeding (e.g. UGH-syndrome, haematological alterations, iris abnormalities) in the anterior chamber or long-standing blood in the vitreous can cause IOP elevation.

Red blood cells (hyphaema) or haemoglobin-laden macrophages along with red blood cells debris (haemolytic glaucoma) or degenerated red blood cells (ghost cell glaucoma) cause TM dysfunction.

Features :

* – Pain and eye irritation
* – Elevated IOP is more common with larger hyphaemas and is more often due to recurrent haemorrhage or re-bleeding
* – “Ghost cells” are degenerated erythrocytes which assume a spherical shape and a khaki colour, which occur 1 to 4 weeks after a vitreous haemorrhage (secondary to either trauma, retinal disease or intraocular surgery) and migrate through a disrupted anterior hyaloid surface in the anterior chamber, where they may be seen circulating or layering over the inferior part of TM at gonioscopic examination. Intraocular haemorrhages may also cause haemolytic glaucoma, in which red-tinged cells in the AH and reddish brown pigmented deposits of the TM are present. Overall, the clinical pictures of ghost-cell glaucoma and haemolytic glaucoma are similar
* – Always exclude angle neovascularization, especially in case of vitreous haemorrage and history of diabetes or previous retinal vascular diseases

Treatment :

* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication as needed. It is recommended to avoid carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and hyperosmotic agents in patients with sickle cell disease
* – Conservative treatment, bed rest, topical cycloplegics and steroids, can be considered for uncomplicated hyphaema. Antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid can reduce the risk of rebleeding. However it is not clear whether any of the interventions have an effect on visual acuity
* – Wash-out through a paracentesis of the anterior chamber and/or vitrectomy to remove RBCs from vitreous if IOP remains high with the risk of corneal blood staining and/or optic neuropathy
* – Consider intravitreal anti-VEGF in case of retinal vascular disease as the cause of vitreous bleeding. Care should be taken to control IOP spikes

###### II.2.3.1.5 Uveitic glaucoma

Aetiology/mechanism :

In acute uveitis, the IOP often drops, probably due to a combination of reduced aqueous production caused by inflammation of the ciliary body and an increased uveoscleral outflow caused by prostaglandin release. However, IOP increase and secondary glaucoma may develop during the course of the disease.

Chronic IOP elevation is typical for Fuchs’ Heterochromic Uveitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Behçet disease, pars planitis, sympathetic ophthalmia, sarcoidosis and syphilis. Acute IOP elevation may also occur and it is typical of Posner-Schlossman syndrome or viral infections such as herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus and cytomegalovirus.

Features :

* – Obstruction and dysfunction of the TM are caused by inflammatory cells, precipitates, debris, secondary scarring and neovascularisation of the chamber angle. Inflammation of the TM or trabeculitis has been proposed in Posner-Schlossman and viral keratouveitis to explain the disproportion of IOP increase and degree of visible anterior segment inflammation
* – Secondary angle closure may develop due to synechial closure of the chamber angle or seclusio pupillae with subsequent iris bombé and appositional angle closure (see Ch II.2.5.1 )
* – Corticosteroid treatment can also contribute to IOP elevation in some patients

Treatment :

* – The goal is the simultaneous treatment of both uveitis and IOP elevation
* – Topical and systemic anti-inflammatory therapy according to the underlying disease
* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication
* – Joint management with uveitis specialist especially for complex cases (e.g. for patients with corticosteroid-induced IOP elevation in order to adequately control the inflammation by other immunosuppresive drugs)
* – Consider aqueous humour analysis to confirm/exclude viral infection in selected patients
* – Ensure adequate antiviral (usually systemic) treatment when viral infection is suspected or confirmed by AH analysis
* – Traditionally topical β-blockers and CAIs have been used as first-line treatment
* – PGAs can be used therapy in eyes with well controlled uveitis
* – Laser trabeculoplasty should be avoided in the acute phase

Acute IOP elevation with corneal oedema but open angle may result from Posner-Schlossman syndrome (iridocyclitic crisis), or from endotheliitis/trabeculitis as in herpetic or cytomegalovirus eye disease.

###### II.2.3.1.6 Neovascular glaucoma

**(see also II.2.5.2.1)**

###### II.2.3.1.7 Glaucoma due to intraocular tumours

Aetiology/mechanism :

Reduced AH outflow due to primary or secondary intraocular tumours, mainly of the anterior segment.

Infiltration of the TM by the tumour or tumour cells floating in the AH. TM obstruction due to tumour related inflammation, tumour debris, haemorrhage or pigment dispersion. Secondary ACG may also develop.

Features :

* – Elevated IOP
* – A highly variable clinical picture, combining evidence of both tumour and glaucoma

Treatment :

* – Treatment of underlying tumour (irradiation, surgical tumour excision, enucleation)
* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication; medical therapy is often first-line treatment while awaiting definitive treatment
* – Cyclodestructive procedures
* – Incisional glaucoma surgery indicated only after successful tumour control

##### II.2.3.2 Secondary open angle glaucoma due to ocular trauma

Ocular trauma leads to glaucoma by several different mechanisms. The secondary traumatic glaucomas can be caused by both open angle and angle closure mechanisms. In order to identify and treat the causes of IOP elevation; careful evaluation of the ocular damage must be performed (See Ch I.1.2.1.2 ).

Aetiology/mechanism :

Blunt non-penetrating or penetrating trauma to the eye can damage intraocular structures.

Any trauma can lead to reduced trabecular outflow due to traumatic changes of the TM (scarring and inflammation, angle recession).

Hyphema is the most common complication following blunt-non penetrating trauma. Vitreous hemorrhages hemolytic hyphema associated with perforating/penetrating or non-perforating/non-penetrating trauma may lead to ghost cell/hemolytic glaucoma (see Ch II.2.3.1.4 ).

Lens induced glaucoma is also possible (see Ch II.2.3.1.3 ).

Features :

* – Elevated IOP may be acute (usually related to obstruction of the TM by red blood cells but also possible without hyphema due to inflammatory cells/debris blockage of the TM) or occur late (e.g after 2-3 weeks like in ghost cell glaucoma) and also a very long time after the trauma (years, like in case of angle recession)
* – Clinical features depend on the aetiology of the trauma
* – Rebleeding in the anterior chamber may occur after 3-7 days as the initial clot begins to retract and lyse
* – Gonioscopy is essential to identify angle recession or other post-traumatic alterations but it is not recommended in fresh ocular trauma (it can be delayed for some weeks)

Treatment :

* – Anti-inflammatory medication
* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication
* – Surgery (anterior chamber washout) if the IOP remains elevated despite medical treatment or there is risk of corneal staining or in case of lens damage
* – Long-term IOP lowering and/or follow-up in the presence of permanent anterior segment damage (as a general rule, patients with angle recession and normal IOP should be examined annually for life)
* – Glaucoma surgery when medical treatment alone does not allow adequate IOP control
* – Consider pausing anti-coagulation if possible and the use of anti-fibrinolytic agents

##### II.2.3.3 Iatrogenic secondary open angle glaucoma

###### II.2.3.3.1 Glaucoma due to corticosteroid treatment

Aetiology/mechanism :

Topical and intravitreal corticosteroid are evidence-based risk factors for IOP increase. Long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy also with nasal sprays, inhalers or periocular skin formulations may also affect IOP. The risk of IOP elevation depends on the chemical structure (strength) of the steroid, dose, frequency and duration of therapy, and route of administration.

Corticosteroids induce changes in the trabecular extracellular matrix (glycoproteins) which lead to decreased outflow facility. A _TIGR_ gene may be involved.

Features :

* – Elevated IOP usually develops 2 to 6 weeks after initiating corticosteroids, but may occur at any time
* – Usually IOP elevation is slowly reversed after stopping the use of corticosteroid

Treatment :

* – Discontinuation of corticosteroid therapy is recommended if possible; steroid-sparing therapy of underlying condition should be considered. If this is not possible, consider switching to weaker steroid (e.g. loteprednol, fluorometholone)
* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication
* – Laser trabeculoplasty
* – Glaucoma surgery may be performed in intractable cases

###### II.2.3.3.2 Secondary open angle glaucoma due to anterior segment ocular surgery and laser

Ocular surgery can cause IOP increase and eventually glaucomatous optic nerve damage by some of the mechanisms discussed above: intraocular haemorrhage, inflammatory reaction, lens material, pigmentary loss from uveal tissue, or trauma.

Aetiology/mechanism :

IOP elevation after anterior segment intraocular surgery is usually transient and is a result of reduced TM outflow which may be caused by: viscoelastic material, inflammatory debris, vitreous in the anterior chamber after cataract surgery, lens particles, prostaglandin release and fibrosis if not properly treated.

Acute onset secondary IOP elevation after neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) LPI, capsulotomy and laser trabeculoplasty. IOP elevation is usually transient, within the first 24 hours, most frequent in the first 4 hours after treatment.

Treatment :

* – Topical and systemic IOP-lowering medication
* – Anti-inflammatory treatment
* – Anterior chamber paracentesis immediately reduces the IOP and can be performed
* – Removal of lens material (timing based on severity, duration and response to medical treatment of inflammation and IOP increase)
* – Removal of the intraocular lens may be needed in case of UGH syndrome
* – Glaucoma surgery according to the specific condition

###### II.2.3.3.3 Glaucoma associated with vitreoretinal surgery

Aetiology/mechanism :

IOP elevation after vitreoretinal surgery may be due to either open angle and angle closure mechanisms. IOP elevation with open angle may develop after vitrectomy with tamponading substances implantation, generally described as silicone oil induced glaucoma, as a result of:

* – Migration of silicone oil into anterior chamber and obstruction of the TM (early post-op IOP increase) usually due to overfill of oil
* – Migration of emulsified silicone oil into anterior chamber with obstruction of TM where oil particles are partially phagocytosed by macrophages and accumulate in the TM especially in the upper quadrant and can induce trabeculitis (intermediate and late onset IOP increase)
* – Prolonged contact of silicone oil with the TM may cause permanent structural changes. Risk factors for developing IOP elevation following vitrectomy with silicone oil implantation include pre-existing OHT or glaucoma, diabetes mellitus, and aphakia (closed angle type)

Treatment :

* – Topical and systemic IOP-lowering medication
* – Anti-inflammatory treatment
* – Removal of silicone oil may be considered in eyes with IOP elevation secondary to silicone oil emulsification. However current data suggest that removal of silicone oil is not effective in all cases and the risk of re-detachment increases
* – Trans-scleral cyclophotocoagulation and aqueous drainage devices seem to represent more effective options, although the latter are associated with the risk of silicone oil escape into subconjuctival space
* – Endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation in eyes requiring silicone oil removal and glaucoma treatment is another option
* – Conventional filtration surgery is associated with poor prognosis

##### II.2.3.4 Secondary open angle glaucoma caused by extraocular disease

###### II.2.3.4.1 Glaucoma caused by increased episcleral venous pressure

Aetiology/mechanism :

Episcleral, orbital or systemic diseases can cause the elevation of episcleral venous pressure with subsequent reduction of trabecular outflow and IOP elevation. The following disorders can be described:

* – Episcleral and orbital causes: chemical burn or radiation damage of the episcleral veins, hemangioma in Sturge-Weber syndrome, naevus of Ota, endocrine orbitopathy, orbital (retrobulbar) tumour, pseudotumour, orbital phlebitis, orbital or intracranial arteriovenous fistula
* – Neurological conditions: dural shunts, cavernous sinus thrombosis
* – Other systemic causes: superior vena cava obstruction, jugular vein obstruction (radical neck dissection), pulmonary venous obstruction
* – Idiopathic forms

Features :

IOP elevation can be acute with eye irritation and pain. Dilated, congested episcleral veins, chemosis, facial lymphoedema, orbital bruit can be present. Vascular bruits are characteristic signs of A/V fistulae.

Treatment :

* – Treatment of the underlying disease
* – Topical and systemic IOP-lowering medication
* – Glaucoma surgery

See Fc II

#### II.2.4 Angle closure

Angle closure refers to closure of the iridocorneal angle due to contact between the iris and trabecular meshwork. It is usually defined by iridotrabecular contact (ITC) of ≥180 degrees. ITC may be appositional (reversible with indentation gonioscopy or with pupil constriction due to light or miotics) or synechial. Gonioscopy is the definitive test for diagnosis of angle closure. Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT) may be used as a supplementary test, e.g. for triage, but it cannot replace gonioscopy for diagnosis. AS-OCT tends to identify more ITC than gonioscopy. Though angle closure increases the risk of glaucoma, angle closure glaucoma is only present when there is both significant ITC and glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

Primary angle closure is the most common subtype of angle closure, but ITC may also occur secondary to anomalies of the iris, lens or due to factors posterior to the lens. Acute angle closure, which can cause sudden visual loss, is an emergency, however the majority of angle closure glaucoma has a gradual onset and is typically asymptomatic in its early stages. In all cases of angle closure it is essential to establish the mechanism and consider possible precipitating medications.

Mechanism

Angle closure can be classified by the mechanism leading to iridotrabecular contact into 4 categories listed from anterior to posterior: 1) at the level of the pupil, 2) at the level of the ciliary body, 3) at the level of lens, and 4) factors behind the lens. Anterior mechanisms (1 and 2) and posterior mechanisms (3 and 4) should be differentiated due to key differences in management. Of note, treatment with miotics for angle closure due to pupil block may worsen angle closure due to posterior mechanisms. See Fc X, XI, XII.

* **I. Pupillary block**
  
  Obstruction at the level of the pupil is the most common mechanism of angle closure, accounting for up to 75% of cases. Pupillary block is an exaggeration of a physiological phenomenon in which the aqueous flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil to the anterior chamber without any resitance. When some resistance to such flow arises, usually at the pupil causing pressure to be higher in the posterior chamber compared to anterior chamber, the iris bows forward and the peripheral iris may touch the trabecular meshwork (TM) causing irido-trabecular contact (ITC). The peripheral and mid-peripheral anterior chamber is typically shallow with the central anterior chamber relatively deep. Pupillary block may also contribute to secondary angle closure, e.g. in case of pupil seclusion induced by uveitis leading to iris bombèe causing 360-degree posterior synechiae.

* **II. At the level of ciliary body**
  
  Angle closure may also occur due to anterior non-pupil block mechanisms such as plateau iris. See Fig II.1.5 .
  
  _Plateau iris configuration_ is characterised by appositional ITC with a flat iris configuration. The peripheral anterior chamber is shallow, but the central AC is typically deep, with the double hump sign visible on dynamic gonioscopy (See gonioscopy chapter). This is due to anteriorly placed ciliary processes pushing the peripheral iris forward, visible as a peripheral hump. Anteriorly positioned ciliary body processes can occur with co-existing pupil block which can push forward the iris causing the double hump. Relief of the pupillary block component using laser iridotomy may be required to identify plateau iris.
  
  Plateau iris syndrome refers to a situation where a patent iridotomy was used to eliminate the pupillary block component but appositional ITC persists. Angle closure in emmetropic or myopic younger people (≤40 years) should raise high suspicion of plateau iris. Pupil block and plateau iris mechanisms may coexist.

* **III. At the level of the lens**
  
  The lens plays an important role in the mechanism of pupil block, but the term lens-induced angle closure is reserved for about 5% of cases where the lens is the unique cause. For example:
* – White or intumescent cataract, e.g., delayed diagnosis or post-trauma
* – Lens subluxation with anterior displacement, e.g., PXF, Marfan syndrome or trauma
* In lens-induced angle closure the anterior chamber tends to be uniformly shallow.

* **IV. Posterior to the lens**
  
  Aqueous misdirection, also called malignant glaucoma, is an uncommon form of angle closure. The mechanism is uncertain but likely involves increased choroidal volume and impaired fluid movement from posterior to anterior segments with posterior misdirection of aqueous possibly accumulating in the vitreous. The lens/ iris diaphragm is pushed forward and occludes the anterior chamber angle. The anterior chamber is uniformly very shallow. Aqueous misdirection usually occurs after surgery in eyes with short axial length. IOP may be normal at early stages.
* – Other posterior pushing mechanism, e.g. tumour, retinal gas or oil tamponade, uveal effusion (e.g. spontaneous, drug-induced) may cause angle closure by forward movement of the lens-iris diaphragm which may be variably combined with pupillary block.

##### II.2.4.1 Primary angle closure glaucoma

Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) affects approximately 20 million people globally, compared to 60 million with POAG. PACG disproportionally accounts for 50% of glaucoma blindness, thus showing a higher rate of visual loss than POAG. The prevalence of PACG in white European adults aged over 40 years is approximately 0.4% (incidence 2-5/100,000 per year) compared to 2.5% for POAG. PACG therefore accounts for approximately 1 in 6 cases of glaucoma in white European adults. It is more common in Chinese (12-16/100,000 per year) and South and South-east Asian people (6-7/100,000 per year). Patients with suspected glaucoma should be assumed to have angle closure until proved otherwise.

The natural history of PAC disease has three stages:

* 1\. Primary angle closure suspect (PACS)
* • ≥180 degrees of ITC with normal IOP and no peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) and no evidence of glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
* 2\. Primary angle closure (PAC)
* • ≥180 degrees of ITC in combination with raised IOP and/or PAS. There is no evidence of glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
* 3\. Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG)
* • ≥180 degrees of ITC with glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

Clinical features :

Most patients with angle closure are asymptomatic. Although symptoms of pain, redness, blurring of vision or haloes may help identify those with sub-acute episodes of IOP elevation due to angle closure, the sensitivity and specificity of symptoms for identifying angle closure is very poor.

See Fc XI

Diagnosis :

Gonioscopy is the best technique for confirming ITC and diagnosing angle closure. It is the only method that allows a 360-degree stereoscopic and dynamic assessment of the angle. AS-OCT can provide a supplementary non-contact method for quantifying anterior chamber anatomy, but it cannot replace gonioscopy for diagnosis. Using AS-OCT, identification of the key landmark of the scleral spur may be difficult in some eyes, as may detection of ciliary processes or PAS. AS-OCT tends to identify more ITC than gonioscopy resulting in false positives. AS-OCT may be useful for demonstrating to patients the mechanism of their problem and for documenting changes in angle width after iridotomy.

**FC XI Management of primary angle closure**

Limbal anterior chamber depth (LACD) (≤25%) or Van Herick test (grade 2) at the temporal limbus has high sensitivity and specificity for angle closure. See Fig. II.1.8 .

A Cochrane review found a LACD threshold of ≤25% had a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.83 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.90) and 0.88 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.92) respectively, however there is a need for high quality studies to evaluate the performance of AS-OCT and LACD and to evaluate their role as triage tests.

Provocative tests for angle closure are not recommended. Provocation with pharmacological dilation of the pupil does not mimic physiological conditions and there is no good quality evidence that pharmacological or dark prone provocation tests are useful for identifying high risk individuals. See Fc X and XI.

Risk factors :

Risk factors for the spectrum of PAC disease include older age, family history, hypermetropia, and race, being more common in Inuits and South and East Asians e.g. Chinese. Three-quarters of cases occur in females. Other factors associated with PAC include a thick peripheral iris, a more anterior iris insertion, and more prominent and anterior lens vault. PXF may also be associated with PACG, probably due to zonular instability. In most cases, the predisposition to pupillary block and angle closure is due to a small anterior segment and to the age-related increased lens volume. Though there is a relationship between hypermetropia and PAC, angle closure also occurs in myopes, and refraction should not be used to determine which patients are assessed for risk of PAC. The COL11A1 gene (the gene related to Stickler’s syndrome) is associated with increased risk of angle closure disease. Angle closure is also associated with connective diseases including Marfan/Weill Marchesani syndrome and Ehler-Danlos syndrome and ocular diseases including retinitis pigmentosa and Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy. First-degree relatives of those with angle closure glaucoma should have regular eye examinations.

Treatment :

Treatment options for pupil block/PAC disease include LPI or due to the central role of the lens, cataract surgery or lens extraction (for high-risk cases). If there is symptomatic cataract, prompt cataract surgery is recommended. There is no evidence to support clear lens extraction for preventing glaucomatous visual loss in PACS or low risk PAC. Medical treatment for elevated IOP should be accompanied by a laser or surgical intervention to reverse ITC and reduce the risk of irreversible damage to the trabecular meshwork. See Ch I.2.2 and I.2.4 .

* – Jindal A, Ctori I, Virgili G, Lucenteforte E, Lawrenson JG. Non-contact tests for identifying people at risk of primary angle closure glaucoma. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020 May 28;5(5):CD012947. doi: 10.1002/14651858.CD012947.pub2. PMID: 32468576; PMCID: PMC7390269.

###### II.2.4.1.1 Primary angle closure suspect (PACS)

Risk of progression :

The short to medium term risk of progression to acute angle closure or to PACG in people with PACS and no other abnormality is low. In a Chinese population, the ZAP study found 36 of 889 untreated eyes with PACS progressed to develop PAS (30 eyes), elevated IOP (5 eyes) or acute angle closure (5 eyes) over 6 years. No patients developed glaucomatous optic neuropathy. This equates to a risk of acute angle closure in those with PACS and no other risk factors of around 1/1000 per year. At 14 years, 105 of 889 untreated eyes had reached one of these primary endpoints, however, almost all were due to PAS (98 PAS, 6 raised IOP, 5 acute angle closure). In the ANA- LIS study, also performed in a Chinese population of PACS eyes, the incidence rate for developmed for PAC or PACG was 21.84/1000 eyes per year in the control group. Older age and higher post dilatation IOP were associated with an increased risk.

However, patients seen at tertiary referral centres may represent more advanced cases with respect to ocular biometrics parameters and may be at higher risk compared to ZAP or ANA-LIS trial participants. See Ch I.2.2 .

Treatment :

Treatment options for PACS include observation or LPI. In the ZAP study, LPI halved the risk of new angle closure disease (defined as raised IOP and/or new PAS) at 6 years but the rate was low, even in untreated eyes, and there were no cases of glaucoma. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of raised IOP and/or new PAS was 44 over 6 years. Similarly, in the ANA-LIS trial, the overall progression rate to PAC or PACG was very low and untreated PACS eyes had twice the risk of developing endpoints, mostly PAS, over 5 years. The NNT benefit of prophylactic LPI for PAC and/ or PACG in the ANA-LIS study was 22 patients to prevent a single endpoint in 1 patient over 5 years.

LPI is not needed for all PACS but is recommended for people with PACS and additional risk factors, including high hypermetropia, family history of angle closure glaucoma, conditions requiring pupil dilation due to the risk of precipitating acute angle closure, use of anticholinergic medications, vulnerable adults who may not report symptoms of angle closure, people with only one eye or those living in remote areas without access to urgent eye care. Patients with untreated PACS should be advised to have regular eye examinations and avoid pharmacologic pupil dilatation. Information should be provided about symptoms of acute angle closure with advice given to seek prompt attention should they occur. Following LPI, it is important to repeat gonioscopy and reevaluate the angle. Persistence of ITC after LPI may be useful to risk stratify patients. Gonioscopy should be repeated in phakic patients even after LPI since the angle will progressively narrow with age-related enlargement of the lens.

###### II.2.4.1.2 Primary angle closure (PAC)

Treatment :

Treatment options for PAC include LPI, or for high-risk PAC, lens extraction. The EAGLE study showed lens extraction was superior to LPI for patients ≥50 years with high- risk PAC (IOP ≥30 mmHg) or PACG. There is no good quality evidence regarding the optimal initial treatment for young patients with PAC or with PAC and IOP <30 mmHg without symptomatic cataract, however, LPI +/- medication is likely the best option. The decision whether to recommend clear lens extraction for PAC should be based on the estimated risk of vision-threatening angle closure versus the risks of surgery. The risk of complications from intraocular surgery is higher in eyes with short axial length (AL), especially when AL ≤20 mm (e.g. aqueous misdirection, capsular rupture). There is an increased lifetime risk of retinal detachment with lens extraction in young patients. The impact of surgery on quality of life should also be considered, including loss of accommodation.

###### II.2.4.1.3 Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG)

Treatment :

If there is symptomatic cataract, prompt cataract surgery is recommended. Removal of the lens will resolve pupil block and if angle closure is appositional reverse ITC. The addition of goniosynechialysis (GSL) has no benefit compared to phacoemulsification alone. If there is PACG and no symptomatic cataract, clear lens extraction should be considered, particularly for patients ≥50 years of age. LPI is an alternative option with a lower procedure-related risk compared to lens extraction, but is likely to be less effective, particularly if there has been prolonged ITC or where there is PAS. Patients with PACG treated with LPI are likely to require continued topical medications for IOP control. Laser peripheral iridoplasty has been suggested for eyes with persistent appositional ITC after LPI, however there is insufficient evidence to recommend. The medical treatment of PACG is similar to POAG with prostaglandin analogues typically first line. Miotics can be used but are not usually tolerated long-term due to their side effects. The angle typically widens after phacoemulsificationemulsification making placement of trabecular MIGS devices technically possible; there is limited evidence of efficacy. See Fc X, Fc XI and Fc XII.

Natural history after phacoemulsification : Once phacoemulsification has been performed, if the angle is open, management is similar to that of POAG. However, if subsequent filtration surgery is considered, the axial length should guide assessment of risk.

**Primary Angle Closure and Risk**

In PACS, high risk may refer to an increased likelihood of acute angle closure due to factors as frequent pupil dilation or the use of antidepressant medications. In PACG, high risk might indicate a greater chance of visual disability, influenced by factors such as younger age, advanced disease, or high IOP.

###### II.2.4.1.4 Acute angle closure (AAC)

Acute angle closure is an emergency. If an acute attack is identified and treated promptly there may be no permanent visual sequelae, however, treatment delay can lead to devastating visual loss within a short period.

Aetiology/mechanism :

In some cases, iridotrabecular contact can lead to a profound reduction in aqueous outflow and acute IOP elevation to very high levels, e.g. up to 50-70 mmHg. Increased resistance to transpupillary aqueous flow due to increased contact between the iris and the lens probably results from a mid-dilated pupil with co-activation of both sphincter and dilator muscles. This may occur in response to physiological stimuli, e.g. low light levels, or pharmacological.

Pupillary block is the most common mechanism, but it is crucial to exclude secondary causes of angle closure (e.g., plateau iris, aqueous misdirection). Whilst pupil-block is treated with pilocarpine, lens-induced and retro-lenticular causes of acute angle closure should be treated with cycloplegia (e.g. atropine, tropicamide or cyclopentolate) and may be worsened by pilocarpine. Typically AAC will not resolve spontaneously.

Features :

* – Ocular pain and frontal headache
* – Decreased visual acuity, blurred vision, ‘haloes’ around lights
* – Variable ‘vagal’ systemic symptoms (nausea and vomiting, abdominal cramps, bradycardia or arrhythmia)
* – Venous congestion and ciliary injection
* – Markedly high IOP
* – Corneal oedema, initially mostly epithelial
* – Pupil mid-dilated and reduced reactivity to light (+/iris atrophy)
* – Shallow peripheral anterior chamber (with iris bombé if pupil block mechanism)
* – Gonioscopy showing extensive ITC (may be difficult to visualise initially due to corneal oedema)
* – Gonioscopy of fellow eye typically showing eye at risk of acute angle closure
* – Glaucomflecken - anterior subcapsular grey-white fleck like opacities due to punctate necrosis of the lens epithelium
* – Fundus: the disc may be normal or show glaucomatous excavation; there may be disc oedema with venous congestion and retinal haemorrhages

Treatment :

Examine the patient and take a focused history to exclude secondary, lens-induced or retro-lenticular causes. As a high proportion of acute angle closure episodes are precipitated by either topical or systemic medications, it is essential to take a thorough history of prescription and non-prescription medications and determine any medication allergies. Topical and systemic medication should be given to lower IOP and help clear the cornea. See Fc XIII.

**_Systemic medication_**

_A:_ Immediate acetazolamide is recommended if IOP ≥ 40 mmHg, preferably intravenously (Intravenous 10 mg/kg) if the patient is vomiting or when rapid onset of action is required. Acetazolamide reduces aqueous production. It should be avoided if there is a history of allergy to sulphonamides or if the patient has severe kidney disease. Potential serious side effects of acetazolamide, particularly in systemically unstable patients, include hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis and dyspnoea. Stevens-Johnson syndrome has also been reported but is extremely rare.

_B:_ Intravenous mannitol (0.5 to 1.5g/kg body weight as a 15% or 20% solution delivered intravenously at 3 to 5 mL/minute) can be considered if there is an inadequate response to acetazolamide. Mannitol lowers IOP through its hyperosmotic effects leading to dehydration of the vitreous body. Patients must be evaluated for heart or kidney disease because hyperosmotics increase blood volume which increases the load in the heart. This may lead to serious systemic risks in some patients, including dehydration, fluid overload, pulmonary oedema, heart failure, electrolyte imbalance, acute kidney injury and subdural haematomas. It is essential to consider the systemic risks of mannitol, and it is not advisable to administer it repeteadly.

**_Topical medication_**

Immediate treatment of AAC should include topical IOP lowering medications with aqueous suppressants preferrable. Prostaglandin analogues have a slower onset of action and are less useful in the acute setting. If pupil block is suspected topical pilocarpine 2% should be given. Pilocarpine may be ineffective if IOP is markedly raised, or the iris is ischaemic so should be deferred until IOP is reduced if presenting IOP is ≥40 mmHg. Pupil constriction tends to occur only when IOP has been lowered. Miotics in large doses can cause systemic side effects including abdominal spasms and sweating; therefore intensive use of pilocarpine should be avoided. Pilocarpine can also cause forward movement of the iris-lens diaphragm, further shallowing the anterior chamber and is contraindicated in lens- induced and retro-lenticular mechanisms of angle closure. In these eyes, cycloplegia rather than miotics, is indicated. Intensive topical steroid e.g., 6 times per day is recommended to reduce inflammation.

**_Laser and surgical treatment_**

_A: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI)_

LPI should be performed as soon as the cornea is sufficiently clear. LPI is firmly indicated in the fellow eyes if they are phakic, ideally at the time of treatment of the acute attack and before discharge. If there is insufficient response to medical treatment and LPI, or if IOP remains high and LPI is not possible due to persistent corneal oedema, surgical iridectomy or cyclodiode laser can be considered.

_B: Laser peripheral iridoplasty_

Iridoplasty may also be used an early intervention for acute angle closure and can break an acute attack as swiftly as medical therapy. Iridoplasty has greater penetration of an oedematous cornea compared to LPI and is an option for when there is persistent corneal oedema preventing LPI or if medical therapy has not lowered IOP quickly (e.g. with 1-2 hours). If iridoplasty is successful in breaking the acute attack, LPI is still required once the cornea has cleared.

_C: Anterior chamber paracentesis for globe decompression_

Paracentesis is an option to immediately lower IOP and break an acute attack, especially in cases refractory to medical therapy or where there is no access to laser. Experienced ophthalmologists can perform paracentesis at the slit lamp, requiring caution since such eyes usually have extremely shallow AC. Complications include excessive shallowing of the anterior chamber, puncture of the iris or lens and suprachoroidal haemorrhage, the latter due to a too rapid decompression of the globe.

The IOP-lowering benefit may quickly wear off and anti-glaucoma medications are necessary to maintain IOP control.

Paracentesis will not resolve pupil block directly but can allow the cornea to clear rapidly and sufficiently for for LPI.

_D: Lens extraction_

After breaking the acute attack, early lens extraction should be considered as soon as the eye is quiet, particularly in cases of high IOP, and persistent ITC after LPI. If all fails lens extraction can also be performed to break an acute attack. If there is corneal oedema, debridement of the epithelium can improve the surgical view. Intraocular surgery in eyes with very high IOP though carries a risk of suprachoroidal haemorrhage due to sudden decompression.

Phacoemulsification following acute angle closure is generally challenging due to the shallow AC, large lens, corneal oedema, poorly dilated pupil, frequent posterior synechiae, lower corneal endothelial cell counts and weaker zonules. It is useful to perform biometry (e.g. axial length, AC depth) following acute angle closure to better understand the anatomical predisposition contributing to the acute attack and gauge the risk of surgery. Eyes with previous acute angle closure undergoing cataract surgery have a higher rate of complications including aqueous misdirection, refractive surprise and corneal decompensation.

_E: Glaucoma surgery_

Phacoemulsification is recommended as initial surgical treatment for PACG, however, though lens extraction can reverse ITC and restore normal IOP, aqueous outflow may be permanently reduced by PAS or non-synechial damage to the TM. Long term IOP lowering medication may be required even after lens extraction and in some further glaucoma surgery is needed. Trabeculectomy or phacoemulsification-trabeculectomy can be considered in severe disease. Caution should be taken with bleb-forming procedures in eyes with short axial length. Cyclophotocoagulation is also a useful option.

###### II.2.4.1.5 Status post-acute angle closure

After acute angle closure the following signs may be present:

Features :

* – Patchy iris atrophy/iris torsion/spiralling
* – Posterior synechiae
* – Pupil either poorly reactive or non-reactive
* – Glaucomflecken
* – Peripheral anterior synechiae
* – Even without synechiae, the TM can be damaged with reduced outflow
* – Decreased corneal endothelial cell count
* – Zonules are often weak
* – The disc may become pale but flat, suggesting an anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, or it can show the typical glaucomatous optic disc neuroretinal rim loss.

In case of lens extraction, precautions and risks are as listed above in Ch II.2.4.1 \- 2 \- 3 \- 4 .

**Pharmacological mydriasis and systemic drugs with effects on the angle**

_Systemic drugs_

Systemic drugs that may induce acute angle closure include nebulised bronchodilators (ipratropium bromide and/or salbutamol), selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, muscle relaxants, illegal stimulant drugs, and other agents with a parasympatholytic and sympathomimetic action. Pharmacologically induced angle closure normally occurs in anatomically predisposed eyes (e.g. shallow anterior chamber). Topiramate and sulfonamides can cause acute angle closure due to peripheral uveal effusion causing a posterior pushing mechanism. Acute angle closure can also occur during or after general anaesthesia.

_Pharmacological mydriasis_

Acute angle closure may occur secondary to pharmacological pupil dilation, however, in the overall population it is generally safe. The risk of missing sight- threatening retinal conditions because of inadequate fundal examination through undilated pupils far outweighs the risk of precipitating angle closure induced by diagnostic mydriasis. However, people undergoing pupil dilatation should be advised to seek eye care urgently in case of symptoms e.g. eye pain. Pupil dilation is usually safe in patients with a known diagnosis of angle closure who have had appropriate prophylactic treatment (e.g. in the presence of a patent iridotomy). Pilocarpine should not be used to preventively re-constrict the pupil after dilation as it may immobilize the pupil in a mid-dilated position, increasing the risk of angle closure.

_Pandit RJ, Taylor R. Diabet Med. 2000 Oct;17(10):693-9. Mydriasis and glaucoma: exploding the myth. A systematic review._

#### II.2.5 Secondary angle closure

There are many different causes of secondary angle closure, and the clinical signs vary according to the underlying condition.

##### II.2.5.1 Secondary angle closure with pupil block

Aetiology/mechanism:

Pupil block pushes the iris forward to occlude the angle. In iritis or iridocyclitis, the development of posterior synechiae may lead to seclusion of the pupil and absolute pupillary block with consequent iris bombé. Acute secondary angle closure may result.

The following is a limited list of other aetiologies for relative or absolute pupil block:

* – Enlarged, swollen lens (cataract, traumatic cataract)
* – Anterior lens dislocation (trauma, zonular laxity, Weill-Marchesani syndrome, Marfan’s syndrome etc.)
* – Protruding vitreous face or intravitreal silicone oil in aphakia
* – Microspherophakia
* – Miotic-induced pupillary block (also the lens moves forward)
* – IOL-induced pupillary block; anterior chamber IOL, phakic intraocular lens, anteriorly dislocated posterior chamber IOL

Treatment :

Several steps may be considered according to causative mechanisms:

* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication (not sufficient on its own)
* – Topical steroids in case of inflammation
* – Nd:YAG LPI
* – Peripheral surgical iridectomy
* – Lens extraction, vitrectomy
* – Discontinuing miotics in miotic-induced pupillary block
* – Pupillary dilatation
* – Nd:YAG laser synechiolysis of posterior synechiae

##### II.2.5.2 Secondary angle closure with anterior “pulling” mechanism synechial closure without pupillary block

Aetiology/mechanism :

The TM is obstructed by iris tissue or a membrane. The iris and/or a membrane are progressively pulled forward to occlude the angle.

###### II.2.5.2.1 Neovascular glaucoma

The iridotrabecular fibrovascular membrane is induced by ocular microvascular disease with retinal ischemia; initially the neovascular membrane covers the angle, causing a secondary form of OAG, then it contracts, causing synechial angle closure.

Treatment :

For the underlying disease/retinal ischemia

* – Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
* – Retinal ablation with laser or cryoprobe

For raised IOP

* – Topical steroid to reduce inflammation
* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication
* – Topical cycloplegic
* – **Long-tube aqueous drainage devices are generally implanted when incisional surgery is considered**
* – Filtering procedure with antimetabolites, with relatively good prognosis if neovascularisation process is successfully treated and quiescent
* – Cyclodestructive procedures
* – Miotics are contraindicated

Systematic review :

* – Simha A, Aziz K, Braganza A, et Al. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor for neo-vascular glaucoma. Cochrane Database of Syst Rev 2020 Feb 6;2(2):CD007920.

###### II.2.5.2.2 Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome

Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome, with progressive endothelial membrane formation and progressive iridotrabecular adhesion. Typically the PAS are patchy, very anterior, with areas of TM apparently normal. There are different presentations of ICE syndrome according to the involvement of the anterior segment structures. ICE syndrome is unilateral, more common in middle-aged women.

Treatment :

* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medications as needed
* – Filtering procedure, with antimetabolite, has limited success
* – Long-tube aqueous drainage device

###### II.2.5.2.3 Epithelial and fibrous ingrowth after anterior segment surgery or penetrating trauma

Epithelial and fibrous ingrowth after anterior segment surgery or penetrating trauma may lead to the formation of an inflammatory membrane.

Treatment :

* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication as needed
* – Excision, destruction of the immigrated tissue
* – Filtering procedure, with antimetabolite, has limited success
* – Aqueous drainage device
* – Cyclodestruction

###### II.2.5.2.4 Aqueous misdirection or malignant glaucoma

Aetiology/mechanism :

Aqueous misdirection is a rare type of secondary angle closure most commonly encountered after filtering surgery in eyes with PACG. It may occur after any type of intraocular surgery. Typically it occurs after surgery involving shallowing of the anterior chamber in eyes at risk, e.g. after trabeculectomy or lens extraction. Forward movement of the lens iris diaphragm causes angle closure resulting in IOP elevation. Risk factors include small eyes (axial length <21 mm), higher hypermetropic refraction (>+6 D) and PACG. Choroidal expansion and resistance to flow of fluid from the posterior to the anterior segment leads to possible aqueous accumulating posteriorly in the vitreous causing forward displacement of the irido-lens diaphragm and closure of the anterior chamber angle.

Treatment :

Medical treatment

* – Parasympatholytics (atropine or cyclopentolate)
* – Aqueous production suppressants given orally and/or topically
* – Hyperosmotics
* – Miotics are contraindicated

Surgical treatment

* – A patent peripheral iridotomy must be present. If not present, LPI should be performed
* – Phakic: pars plana vitrectomy with or without lens extraction
* – Pseudophakic: Nd:YAG laser vitreolysis/capsulotomy may be tried
* – Pseudophakic: Zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy can be performed using an anterior approach through a peripheral iridectomy
* – Diode laser cyclophotocoagulation can be considered at any time

See Fc X-XI-XII

###### II.2.5.2.5 Iris and ciliary body cysts, intraocular tumours

Treatment :

* – Tumour irradiation or excision
* – Filtering surgery only after the tumour is controlled
* – Cyclodestruction

###### II.2.5.2.6 Silicone oil or other tamponading fluids or gas implanted in the vitreous cavity

Treatment :

* – Topical/systemic IOP lowering medications as needed
* – Topical steroids in case of inflammation
* – Inferior iridectomy
* – Silicone oil or gas aspiration
* – Filtering surgery
* – Long–tube drainage device
* – Cyclodestruction

###### II.2.5.2.7 Uveal effusion

Aetiology/mechanism :

* – Inflammation as in scleritis, uveitis, human immunodeficiency virus infection
* – Increased choroidal venous pressure as in nanophthalmos, scleral buckling, panretinal photocoagulation, central retinal vein occlusion, arterio-venous communication
* – Tumour
* – Drug-induced

Treatment :

* – Attempt to address the underlying mechanism
* – Anti-inflammatory medication as needed
* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medication as needed
* – Relaxation of scleral buckling; vitrectomy, sclerectomy in nanophthalmos
* – Tumour excision or irradiation

###### I.2.5.2.8 Retinopathy of prematurity (Stage V)

Features :

* – Discomfort, pain, redness
* – Corneal oedema
* – IOP ≥21 mmHg
* – Axially shallow anterior chamber

Treatment :

* – Topical and systemic IOP lowering medications
* – Filtering procedure with or without antimetabolite
* – Long–tube drainage devices

###### II.2.5.2.9 Congenital anomalies associated with secondary angle closure glaucoma

These conditions are extremely variable in pathogenesis, clinical presentation and required management; an extensive discussion is outside the scope of this chapter.

Aetiology/mechanism :

Angle closure is caused by pushing forward the ciliary body and iris. Increase of volume of the posterior segment of the eye.

Examples are familial iris hypoplasia, anomalous superficial iris vessels, aniridia, Sturge- Weber syndrome, neurofibromatosis, Marfan’s syndrome, Pierre Robin syndrome, homocystinuria, goniodysgenesis, Lowe’s syndrome, microcornea, microspherophakia, rubella, broad thumb syndrome, persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.

Features :

* – Corneal oedema
* – Axially shallow anterior chamber

Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT) may be used as a supplementary test e.g. for triage, but it cannot replace gonioscopy for diagnosis.

Gonioscopy should be repeated, and the angle reassessed periodically during follow-up in all phakic patients.

Always consider iatrogenic causes of angle closure including prescribed or over the counter medications or remedies.

## Part II • **Chpater 3**

### Treatment

### II.3 Treatment

#### II.3.1 General principles

The goal of care for people with, or at risk of, glaucoma is to promote their well-being and quality of life within a sustainable health care system.

Well-being and quality of life are influenced by a person’s visual function, the psychological impact of having a chronic progressive sight-threatening condition and the costs and side-effects of treatments.

Costs include inconveniences to the individual and their care givers as well as the financial cost of examinations, diagnostic procedures and therapies, both to the individual and to society.

The effect of visual function on well-being and quality of life is variable: in general, early to moderate glaucoma has only a modest influence, whereas advanced visual function loss in both eyes may considerably reduce quality of life.

The only proven method of preserving visual function is to reduce the intraocular pressure (IOP).

Glaucoma is still the second leading cause of blindness in Europe. In most Western countries at least half of patients with manifest glaucoma are undiagnosed and glaucoma is often diagnosed late. A considerable percentage of glaucoma patients, estimated to be more than 10%, become blind in both eyes or encounter serious visual field loss in both eyes within their lifetime. Major risk factors for glaucoma visual disability are the severity of the disease at presentation, bilateral disease and age. A young patient with mild bilateral damage is at a much larger risk of disability in his lifetime than an 80-year- old patient with moderate unilateral disease. Thus, treatment must be individualized to the needs and rate of progression of each patient (see Figure II.3.1 ).

When examining an individual with glaucoma it is assumed that the pre-treatment level of IOP has damaged the optic nerve and will continue to do so. An IOP level is, therefore, identified below which further damage is considered unlikely: this is known as the ‘Target IOP’. The definition of Target IOP is as follows: Target IOP is the upper limit of IOP which is considered to either prevent further damage or to slow the rate of VF deterioration sufficient to maintain the patient’s vision-related QoL during their lifetime. The level of evidence for the concept of setting a Target IOP is low, but the approach is recommended. It is important to adjust the Target IOP when needed based on the rate of visual field worsening and risk of visual disability (see Figure II.3.1 ).

The impact of a loss of QoL resulting from glaucoma should determine target pressure, intensity of treatment and frequency of follow-up. For instance, patients with severe functional loss or younger patients with manifest disease should have more aggressive treatment and closer follow-up than patients with little or no risk, e.g., very old patients with early field loss or unilateral disease. Glaucoma suspects have an even smaller risk of visual impairment.

In most patients with advanced glaucoma and reasonably long life expectancy, aggressive IOP lowering treatment is recommended. Elderly patients with significant health problems and mild glaucoma with relatively low IOP might prefer being followed without treatment. When treatment options are discussed with a patient, general health

status and personal preferences must be considered and respected. It is also important to ensure that patients are able to comply and persist with therapy.

Disease progression rates differ very much between patients and types of glaucoma, from very slow to rapid. Many patients with glaucoma show no or only small deterioration despite years of follow-up, while rapid progression may occur in others, e.g. in patients with PEXG. The likely or observed rate of progression should determine target pressure, treatment intensity and frequency of follow-up (see Ch II.3.3 ). Determining the rate of progression is the standard in glaucoma care. In patients at high risk of losing vision- related QoL, a sufficient number of examinations is required to estimate the rate of progression. Frequent VF testing, e.g., three VF tests per year for the first two years after diagnosis, may be valuable for patients with significant disease to make it possible to identify rapidly progressing glaucoma. If clinically significant progression has not been identified in the first two years, the frequency of tests may be reduced. Such frequent testing is not required for all patients with glaucoma, e.g., elderly with mild disease in one eye and low untreated IOP. Once the progression rate has been determined, the target pressure should be re-evaluated based on the measured rate of progression and concomitant IOP values.

Currently, the only approach proven to be effective in preserving visual function is

lowering IOP (See Part I and Fc VIII , IX XIV ). However, some patients may experience a reduction in visual function despite IOP lowering. There is a need for effective non-IOP related medication. Neuroprotection can be defined as a therapeutic approach which aims to directly prevent neuronal damage. Several compounds have been shown to be neuroprotective in animal models of glaucoma, but none has reached yet a sufficient level of evidence to be considered effective in preserving visual function in glaucoma patients. There is some evidence that neuroprotective compounds may be beneficial for maintaining QoL.

Data from epidemiological studies have shown that some patients over-treated for systemic hypertension may be at increased risk of glaucoma and VF loss. However, there is no conclusive evidence to support the idea that adjusting treatment in an attempt to enhance ocular blood flow can improve the outcome in glaucoma patients.

The goal of glaucoma management is to promote the best possible well-being and quality of life with minimal visual disability caused by glaucoma, within a sustainable health care system. The only approach proven to be effective in preserving visual function is lowering IOP.

Overview of strategies to achieve our goal

* – Identify patients with glaucoma and especially those at risk of severe visual loss.
* – Identify patients at risk of developing glaucoma.
* – Identify the type and mechanism of glaucoma (see Ch II.2 ).
* – Manage and treat according to the expected rate of disease progression and risk of loss of quality of life.
* – Use visual fields to quantify glaucoma stage and progression.
* – In eyes at risk with a normal visual field, structural monitoring can be particularly useful to detect significant changes.
* – Decrease the risk of disease progression.
* – Determine the target IOP for the individual. In general, when there is more advanced damage, lower IOPs are needed to prevent further progression.

IOP lowering with medication/laser/surgery

* – Verify the efficacy of treatment and reassess target IOP (see Ch II.3 ).
* – Monitor the rate of progression (function and structure).
* – Adjust management according to rate of progression and risk of visual disability.
* – Assessment of the iridocorneal angle and for signs of secondary glaucoma is crucial for correct phenotyping and treatment decision.
* – Always evaluate adherence to treatment and monitoring schedule.
* – Audit outcomes e.g. efficacy, safety, use of resources (see Ch I.8 ).
* – Failures include patients suffering from the consequences of insufficient IOP lowering, side effects of medications and surgical complications.

#### II.3.2 Treatment options

The benefits of IOP reduction both in managing glaucoma irrespective of the level of untreated IOP as well as to decrease the risk of conversion of OHT to glaucoma have been well established. Most forms of open angle glaucoma may be initially treated with topical medications or laser trabeculoplasty. Initial surgery may be considered in patients with advanced VF loss at presentation. If IOP does not match the clinical picture it is advisable to repeat the measurement. In cases with very high IOP where IOP lowering treatment is deemed necessary to be initiated on the same day, it is advisable to measure the IOP twice during the visit to ensure reproducibility.

Systematic review:

* – Burr J, Azuara-Blanco A, Avenell A, Tuulonen A. Medical versus surgical interventions for open angle glaucoma. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;(9):CD004399.
* – Rolim-de-Moura CR, Paranhos Jr A, Loutfi M, Burton D, Wormald R, Evans JR. Laser trabeculoplasty for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Cochrane Database SystRev 2022 (PMID: 35943114).

#### II.3.3 Target IOP

Therapy in glaucoma management aims to lower IOP to slow the VF deterioration to a rate sufficient to maintain the patient’s QoL.

Target IOP is the upper limit of IOP judged to be compatible with this treatment goal. It should be re-evaluated regularly and, additionally, when progression-threatening visual disability is identified or when ocular or systemic comorbidities develop.

There is no single target IOP level that is appropriate for every patient, so the target IOP needs to be estimated for each eye of every patient (see Figure II.3.2 ).

##### II.3.3.1 Setting the Target IOP

There is little evidence to support any particular algorithm to set the target IOP.

**FC XIV Target IOP decision-making factors**
